chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 1 — London. A street
paragraphs: [Enter RICHARD, Duke of Gloucester, alone.]

RICHARD. Now is the winter of our discontent made glorious summer by this son of York; and all the clouds that hung threateningly over our house lie buried in the deep bosom of the ocean. Now our brows are bound with victorious wreaths, our battered weapons hung up as monuments, our harsh war-cries turned to merry meetings, our dreadful marches into delightful dances. Grim-faced war has smoothed his wrinkled forehead; and now, instead of mounting armored horses to terrify the souls of fearful enemies, he skips nimbly in a lady's chamber to the lewd, pleasing strumming of a lute. But I, who am not shaped for playful tricks, nor made to court an amorous looking-glass; I, who am roughly stamped, and lack love's majesty to strut before a wanton, ambling nymph; I, who am cheated of fair proportion, robbed of beauty by deceiving nature, deformed, unfinished, sent before my time into this living world scarcely half made up, and so lamely and unfashionably that dogs bark at me as I limp by them — why I, in this weak piping time of peace, have no delight to pass away the time, except to spy my shadow in the sun and comment on my own deformity. And therefore, since I cannot prove a lover to occupy these fair well-spoken days, I am determined to prove a villain, and hate the idle pleasures of these days. I have laid plots, dangerous beginnings, by means of drunken prophecies, libels, and dreams, to set my brother Clarence and the King in deadly hatred against each other; and if King Edward is as true and just as I am subtle, false, and treacherous, this day Clarence should be closely locked up because of a prophecy which says that someone whose name begins with "G" shall be the murderer of Edward's heirs. Dive down, thoughts, into my soul. Here Clarence comes.
[Enter CLARENCE, guarded, and BRAKENBURY.]
Brother, good day. What's the meaning of this armed guard that attends upon Your Grace?
CLARENCE. His Majesty, looking after my personal safety, has appointed this escort to convey me to the Tower.
RICHARD. On what grounds?
CLARENCE. Because my name is George.

RICHARD. Alas, my lord, that fault is none of yours. He should, for that, lock up your godfathers. Oh, perhaps His Majesty intends that you should be re-christened in the Tower. But what's the matter, Clarence? May I know?

CLARENCE. Yes, Richard, when I know myself, for I swear I don't yet. But, as I can gather, he listens to prophecies and dreams, and picks the letter G from the alphabet, and says a wizard told him that someone whose name begins with G shall disinherit his offspring. And because my name George begins with G, it follows in his thinking that I'm the one. These, as I hear, and other such trifles, have moved His Highness to commit me now.

RICHARD. Why, this is what happens when men are ruled by women. It isn't the King who sends you to the Tower; it's my Lady Grey, his wife, Clarence, who pushes him to this extreme. Wasn't it she and that good worshipful man, Antony Woodville her brother, who got him to send Lord Hastings to the Tower, from which he was released only today? We are not safe, Clarence; we are not safe.

CLARENCE. By heaven, I think no man is secure except the Queen's relatives, and the night-walking messengers who scurry between the King and Mistress Shore. Did you not hear what a humble petitioner Lord Hastings was to her for his release?

RICHARD. Humbly begging her divinity got my Lord Chamberlain his freedom. I'll tell you what: I think it's our best course, if we want to stay in favor with the King, to become her men and wear her livery. The jealous worn-out widow and Mistress Shore herself, since our brother dubbed them gentlewomen, are powerful gossips in our monarchy.
BRAKENBURY. I beg both Your Graces to pardon me. His Majesty has strictly ordered that no man, of whatever rank, shall have private conversation with your brother.

RICHARD. Very well; if it please Your Worship, Brakenbury, you may share in anything we say. We speak no treason, man. We say the King is wise and virtuous, and his noble Queen well advanced in years, fair, and not jealous. We say that Shore's wife has a pretty foot, a cherry lip, a bonny eye, a most pleasing tongue; and that the Queen's relatives are made gentlefolk. What do you say, sir? Can you deny any of this?
BRAKENBURY. As for this, my lord, I myself have nothing to do with it.
RICHARD. Nothing to do with Mistress Shore? I tell you, fellow, he that does nothing with her, excepting one man, had best do it secretly and alone.
BRAKENBURY. What one, my lord?
RICHARD. Her husband, fool! Would you betray me?
BRAKENBURY. I beg Your Grace to pardon me, and also to leave off your conversation with the noble Duke.
CLARENCE. We know your orders, Brakenbury, and will obey.

RICHARD. We are the Queen's outcasts and must obey. Brother, farewell. I will go to the King, and whatever you would have me do — were it even to call King Edward's widow "sister" — I will perform it to set you free. Meanwhile, this deep disgrace done to our brotherhood touches me more deeply than you can imagine.
CLARENCE. I know it pleases neither of us.
RICHARD. Well, your imprisonment shall not be long. I will deliver you or else lie in your place. Meanwhile, have patience.
CLARENCE. I must, of necessity. Farewell.
[Exeunt CLARENCE, BRAKENBURY, and guard.]

RICHARD. Go tread the path you shall never return from. Simple, plain Clarence, I love you so dearly that I will shortly send your soul to heaven, if heaven will accept the present from our hands. But who comes here? The newly-released Hastings?
[Enter LORD HASTINGS.]
HASTINGS. Good day to my gracious lord.
RICHARD. As much to my good Lord Chamberlain. You are most welcome to the open air. How has Your Lordship endured imprisonment?
HASTINGS. With patience, noble lord, as prisoners must; but I shall live, my lord, to give thanks to those who were the cause of my imprisonment.
RICHARD. No doubt, no doubt; and so shall Clarence too, for they that were your enemies are his, and have prevailed as much over him as over you.
HASTINGS. The greater pity that eagles should be caged, while kites and buzzards prey at liberty.
RICHARD. What's the news abroad?
HASTINGS. No news abroad so bad as this at home: the King is sickly, weak, and melancholy, and his physicians fear greatly for him.
RICHARD. Now, by Saint John, that news is bad indeed. Oh, he has kept an evil diet a long time, and overly consumed his royal person. It's very grievous to think upon. Where is he, in his bed?
HASTINGS. He is.
RICHARD. You go ahead, and I will follow.
[Exit HASTINGS.]

He cannot live, I hope, and must not die until George is packed off post-haste to heaven. I'll go in to urge his hatred against Clarence still further with lies well-armed with weighty arguments; and if I do not fail in my deep design, Clarence has not another day to live. Once that's done, God take King Edward to his mercy, and leave the world for me to bustle in. For then I'll marry Warwick's youngest daughter. What of it, that I killed her husband and her father? The readiest way to make the wench amends is to become her husband and her father; the which I will do — not so much for love as for another secret close-held intent, which by marrying her I must achieve. But still I run before my horse to market. Clarence still breathes; Edward still lives and reigns. When they are gone, then I must count my gains.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 2 — London. Another street
paragraphs: [Enter the corpse of King Henry VI, with halberdiers guarding it, LADY ANNE as the mourner, TRESSEL and BERKELEY, and other gentlemen.]

ANNE. Set down, set down your honorable load — if honor may be shrouded in a hearse — while for a while I dutifully lament the untimely fall of virtuous Lancaster. Poor key-cold figure of a holy king, pale ashes of the house of Lancaster, you bloodless remnant of that royal blood, may it be lawful for me to invoke your ghost to hear the lamentations of poor Anne, wife to your Edward, to your slaughtered son, stabbed by the very same hand that made these wounds. Look, into these windows that let out your life I pour the helpless balm of my poor eyes. Oh, cursed be the hand that made these holes; cursed the heart that had the heart to do it; cursed the blood that let this blood out from here. May more dreadful misfortune fall on that hated wretch who makes us wretched by your death than I could wish to adders, spiders, toads, or any creeping venomous thing that lives. If ever he has a child, may it be aborted, monstrous, and brought to light before its time, whose ugly and unnatural appearance may frighten the hopeful mother at the sight, and let it be heir to his misery. If ever he has a wife, let her be made more miserable by his death than I am made by my young lord and you. Come now towards Chertsey with your holy load, taken from St. Paul's to be buried there; and whenever you are weary of this weight, rest, while I lament King Henry's corpse.
[They take up the bier.]
[Enter RICHARD, Duke of Gloucester.]
RICHARD. Stop, you that carry the corpse, and set it down.
ANNE. What black magician conjures up this fiend to interrupt devoted, charitable acts?
RICHARD. Villains, set down the corpse, or by Saint Paul I'll make a corpse of him who disobeys!
GENTLEMAN. My lord, stand back, and let the coffin pass.
RICHARD. Ill-mannered dog — you stand still when I command! Raise your halberd higher than my chest, or by Saint Paul I'll strike you to my foot and kick you, beggar, for your boldness.
[They set down the bier.]

ANNE. What, are you trembling? Are you all afraid? Alas, I don't blame you, for you are mortal, and mortal eyes cannot endure the devil. Be gone, you dreadful minister of hell! You only had power over his mortal body; his soul you cannot have; therefore, go.
RICHARD. Sweet saint, for charity's sake, don't be so harsh.

ANNE. Foul devil, for God's sake, away — and don't trouble us; for you have made the happy earth into your hell, filled it with cursing cries and deep groans. If you delight in viewing your hateful deeds, behold this sample of your butcheries. Oh, gentlemen, see, see how dead Henry's wounds open their congealed mouths and bleed afresh! Blush, blush, you lump of foul deformity, for it's your presence that draws this blood from cold and empty veins where no blood dwells. Your deeds, inhuman and unnatural, provoke this flood, which itself is most unnatural. O God, who made this blood, avenge his death! O earth, who drinks this blood, avenge his death! Either let heaven strike the murderer dead with lightning, or let the earth gape open wide and swallow him alive, as you swallow up this good king's blood, which his hell-governed arm has butchered.
RICHARD. Lady, you know no rules of charity, which returns good for bad, blessings for curses.
ANNE. Villain, you know neither the law of God nor of man. No beast is so fierce that it doesn't know some touch of pity.
RICHARD. But I know none, and therefore am no beast.
ANNE. Oh, wonderful, when devils tell the truth!
RICHARD. More wonderful when angels are so angry. Grant me, divine perfection of a woman, leave to clear myself, point by point, of these supposed crimes.
ANNE. Grant me, diffused infection of a man, leave merely to accuse your cursed self, point by point, of these known evils.
RICHARD. Fairer than tongue can name you, let me have some patient leisure to excuse myself.
ANNE. Fouler than heart can think you, you can make no valid excuse but to hang yourself.
RICHARD. By such despair I would accuse myself.
ANNE. And by despairing you shall stand excused, for doing worthy vengeance on yourself, who did unworthy slaughter upon others.
RICHARD. Suppose I didn't kill them?
ANNE. Then suppose they were not killed. But dead they are, and, devilish slave, by you.
RICHARD. I did not kill your husband.
ANNE. Why then he must be alive.
RICHARD. No, he is dead, and killed by Edward's hand.
ANNE. You lie in your foul throat. Queen Margaret saw your murderous sword smoking in his blood — the same sword you once turned against her breast, though your brothers beat the point aside.
RICHARD. I was provoked by her slanderous tongue, that laid their guilt upon my guiltless shoulders.
ANNE. You were provoked by your bloody mind, that never dreams of anything but butcheries. Didn't you kill this King?
RICHARD. I grant you that.
ANNE. You grant me, hedgehog? Then, God grant me too that you may be damned for that wicked deed. Oh, he was gentle, mild, and virtuous.
RICHARD. So much the better for the King of Heaven who has him.
ANNE. He is in heaven, where you shall never come.
RICHARD. Let him thank me — I helped send him there, for he was fitter for that place than for earth.
ANNE. And you are unfit for any place but hell.
RICHARD. Yes, one other place, if you'll hear me name it.
ANNE. Some dungeon.
RICHARD. Your bedchamber.
ANNE. May ill rest befall the chamber where you lie!
RICHARD. So it will, madam, until I lie with you.
ANNE. I hope so.

RICHARD. I know so. But, gentle Lady Anne, to leave this sharp encounter of our wits and turn to a slower manner: isn't the cause of the untimely deaths of these Plantagenets, Henry and Edward, as blamable as the executioner?
ANNE. You were the cause, and the most accursed effect of it.
RICHARD. Your beauty was the cause of that effect: your beauty, that haunted me in my sleep, urging me to undertake the death of all the world, so I might live one hour in your sweet bosom.
ANNE. If I thought that, I tell you, murderer, these nails should tear that beauty from my cheeks.
RICHARD. These eyes could not endure that beauty's destruction; you should not blemish it if I stood by. As all the world is cheered by the sun, so am I by that beauty; it is my day, my life.
ANNE. May black night overshadow your day, and death your life.
RICHARD. Don't curse yourself, fair creature; you are both my day and life.
ANNE. I wish I were, to be revenged on you.
RICHARD. It is a most unnatural quarrel, to be revenged on him who loves you.
ANNE. It is a just and reasonable quarrel, to be revenged on him who killed my husband.
RICHARD. He who deprived you, lady, of your husband did it to help you to a better husband.
ANNE. His better doesn't breathe upon the earth.
RICHARD. He lives who loves you better than your husband could.
ANNE. Name him.
RICHARD. Plantagenet.
ANNE. Why, that was he.
RICHARD. The very same name, but one of better nature.
ANNE. Where is he?
RICHARD. Here.
[She spits at him.]
Why do you spit at me?
ANNE. I wish it were deadly poison, for your sake.
RICHARD. Never came poison from so sweet a place.
ANNE. Never hung poison on a fouler toad. Out of my sight! You infect my eyes.
RICHARD. Your eyes, sweet lady, have infected mine.
ANNE. I wish they were basilisks, to strike you dead!

RICHARD. I wish they were, so I might die at once; for now they kill me with a living death. Those eyes of yours have drawn salt tears from mine, shamed their look with a store of childish drops. These eyes, that never shed a remorseful tear — no, not when my father York and Edward wept to hear the piteous moan that Rutland made when black-faced Clifford shook his sword at him; nor when your warlike father, like a child, told the sad story of my father's death, and twenty times paused to sob and weep, so that all the bystanders had wet cheeks like trees splashed with rain. In that sad time my manly eyes scorned a humble tear; and what those sorrows could not draw out, your beauty has, and made them blind with weeping. I have never pleaded with friend or enemy; my tongue could never learn a sweet, soothing word; but now that your beauty is offered as my prize, my proud heart pleads and prompts my tongue to speak.
[She looks scornfully at him.]

Don't teach your lip such scorn; it was made for kissing, lady, not for such contempt. If your vengeful heart cannot forgive, look, here I lend you this sharp-pointed sword, which if you please to hide in this true breast and let the soul forth that adores you — I lay it bare to the deadly stroke, and humbly beg for death on my knee.
[He kneels and lays his breast open; she offers to stab him with his sword.]
No, do not pause — for I did kill King Henry — but it was your beauty that provoked me. No, now strike; it was I who stabbed young Edward — but it was your heavenly face that set me on.
[She drops the sword.]
Take up the sword again, or take up me.
ANNE. Rise, hypocrite. Though I wish your death, I will not be your executioner.
RICHARD. Then bid me kill myself, and I will do it.
ANNE. I have already.

RICHARD. That was in your rage. Say it again, and at that very word, this hand, which for your love did kill your love, shall for your love kill a far truer love. You shall be accessory to both their deaths.
ANNE. I wish I knew your heart.
RICHARD. It is figured in my tongue.
ANNE. I'm afraid both are false.
RICHARD. Then never was a man true.
ANNE. Well, well, put up your sword.
RICHARD. Then say my peace is made.
ANNE. You shall learn that later.
RICHARD. But shall I live in hope?
ANNE. All men, I hope, do.
RICHARD. Deign to wear this ring.
ANNE. To take is not to give.
[He places the ring on her hand.]

RICHARD. Look how my ring encompasses your finger; even so your breast encloses my poor heart. Wear both of them, for both of them are yours. And if your poor devoted servant may just beg one favor at your gracious hand, you confirm his happiness forever.
ANNE. What is it?

RICHARD. That it may please you to leave these sad arrangements to him who has most reason to be a mourner, and at once go to Crosby Place; where, after I have solemnly buried this noble King at Chertsey monastery, and wet his grave with my repentant tears, I will, with all dutiful haste, come see you. For various unknown reasons, I beg you, grant me this favor.
ANNE. With all my heart — and it gives me much joy to see you have become so penitent. Tressel and Berkeley, come along with me.
RICHARD. Bid me farewell.
ANNE. That's more than you deserve; but since you teach me how to flatter you, imagine I have said farewell already.
[Exeunt LADY ANNE, TRESSEL, and BERKELEY.]
RICHARD. Gentlemen, take up the corpse.
GENTLEMAN. Toward Chertsey, noble lord?
RICHARD. No, to White Friars; wait there for me.
[Exeunt halberdiers and gentlemen with the corpse.]

Was ever a woman wooed in this manner? Was ever a woman won in this manner? I'll have her, but I will not keep her long. What — I, who killed her husband and his father, to take her in the most extreme hatred of her heart, with curses on her mouth, tears in her eyes, the bleeding witness of her hatred nearby, having God, her conscience, and these obstacles against me, and no friends to back my suit at all, but the plain devil and dissembling looks? And yet, to win her — I bet the world against nothing on it! Ha! Has she already forgotten that brave prince, Edward, her lord, whom I, some three months ago, stabbed in my angry mood at Tewkesbury? A sweeter and lovelier gentleman, framed in the lavishness of nature — young, valiant, wise, and no doubt truly royal — the wide world cannot offer again. And will she yet lower her eyes on me, who cut off the golden prime of this sweet prince, and made her a widow to a sorrowful bed? On me, whose whole self does not equal Edward's half? On me, who limps and is misshapen like this? My dukedom against a beggar's penny, I've been misjudging my person all this while! On my life, she finds — although I cannot — that I am a marvelously proper man. I'll go to the expense of a looking-glass, and hire twenty or so tailors to study fashions to adorn my body. Since I have crept into favor with myself, I will maintain it at some small cost. But first I'll dump that fellow into his grave, and then return lamenting to my love. Shine out, fair sun, until I have bought a mirror, so that I may see my shadow as I pass.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 3 — London. A Room in the Palace
paragraphs: [Enter QUEEN ELIZABETH, the Marquess of DORSET, Lord RIVERS, and Lord GREY.]
RIVERS. Have patience, madam. There's no doubt His Majesty will soon recover his usual health.
GREY. The fact that you take it so badly only makes him worse. So, for God's sake, keep up good cheer, and lift His Grace's spirits with quick and merry eyes.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. If he were dead, what would become of me?
GREY. No harm beyond the loss of such a lord.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. The loss of such a lord includes every harm.
GREY. Heaven has blessed you with a fine son to be your comforter when he's gone.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Ah, but he's young, and his minority is entrusted to Richard Gloucester, a man who loves neither me nor any of you.
RIVERS. Has it been settled that he'll be Protector?
QUEEN ELIZABETH. It's decided, though not yet finalized. But it has to be, if the King doesn't survive.
[Enter BUCKINGHAM and STANLEY, Earl of Derby.]
GREY. Here come the Lords of Buckingham and Derby.
BUCKINGHAM. Good day to Your Royal Grace.
STANLEY. May God make Your Majesty as joyful as you have been.

QUEEN ELIZABETH. The Countess Richmond, good my Lord of Derby, will hardly say amen to your kind prayer. Yet, Derby, even though she's your wife and doesn't love me, rest assured, good lord, I don't hate you for her proud arrogance.

STANLEY. I beg you, either don't believe the envious slanders of her false accusers, or if she really is accused on a true report, bear with her weakness, which I think comes from a willful sickness, not from any real malice.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Did you see the King today, my Lord of Derby?
STANLEY. The Duke of Buckingham and I have just come from visiting His Majesty.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. What hope is there of his recovery, my lords?
BUCKINGHAM. Madam, good hope; His Grace speaks cheerfully.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. God grant him health! Did you speak with him?
BUCKINGHAM. Yes, madam. He wants to reconcile the Duke of Gloucester with your brothers, and them with my Lord Chamberlain. He has sent to summon them to his royal presence.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. I wish all were well — but it never will be. I fear our happiness is at its peak.
[Enter RICHARD, Duke of Gloucester, and HASTINGS.]

RICHARD. They do me wrong, and I will not stand for it! Who is it that complains to the King that I, supposedly, am stern and don't love them? By holy Paul, they have little love for His Grace who fill his ears with such divisive rumors. Because I can't flatter and put on a fair face, smile in men's faces, smooth-talk, deceive, and cheat, duck with French nods and apish courtesy, I have to be considered a bitter enemy. Can't a plain man live and mean no harm, without his honest truth being twisted by silken, sly, insinuating Jacks?
GREY. Who in this whole company is Your Grace speaking to?

RICHARD. To you — you who have neither honesty nor grace. When have I injured you? When done you wrong? Or you? Or you? Or any of your faction? A plague on you all! His Royal Grace — whom God preserve better than you would wish — can hardly have a moment's peace before you trouble him with vulgar complaints.

QUEEN ELIZABETH. Brother of Gloucester, you mistake the matter. The King, of his own royal disposition, and not pushed by any other petitioner, aiming, I suppose, at the hidden hatred that your outward actions show against my children, my brothers, and myself, has sent for you so he may learn the cause of your ill will, and then remove it.
RICHARD. I can't say. The world has grown so bad that wrens hunt where eagles dare not perch. Since every Jack has become a gentleman, many a gentle person has been made a Jack.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Come, come, we know what you mean, brother Gloucester. You envy my advancement, and my friends'. God grant we never need you.

RICHARD. Meanwhile, God grants that we do need you. Our brother is imprisoned because of you, I'm disgraced, and the nobility held in contempt, while great promotions are daily given to ennoble those who scarcely two days ago weren't worth a noble.

QUEEN ELIZABETH. By Him who raised me to this anxious height from the contented state I once enjoyed, I never incited His Majesty against the Duke of Clarence — I have been an earnest advocate pleading for him. My lord, you do me shameful injury by falsely drawing me into these vile suspicions.
RICHARD. You may deny that you weren't the cause of my Lord Hastings's recent imprisonment.
RIVERS. She may, my lord, because —

RICHARD. She may, Lord Rivers — who doesn't know that? She may do more than just deny it, sir. She may help you to many fine promotions, and then deny her helping hand in it, and lay those honors on your own high merit. What can't she do? She may, yes, indeed, may she —
RIVERS. What, indeed, may she?
RICHARD. What, indeed, may she? Marry a king — a bachelor, and a handsome young fellow at that. Truly, your grandmother had a worse match.

QUEEN ELIZABETH. My lord of Gloucester, I have endured too long your blunt rebukes and bitter scoffs. By heaven, I'll tell His Majesty about the gross taunts I've often had to endure. I'd rather be a country servant-girl than a great queen on these terms, baited, scorned, and stormed at like this.
[Enter old QUEEN MARGARET, behind.]
Small joy I have in being England's queen.
QUEEN MARGARET.
[Aside.] And may that little joy be lessened — God, I pray!
Your honor, status, and seat are owed to me.

RICHARD. What, do you threaten me with telling the King? Tell him, don't hold back. What I've said, I'll stand by in the King's presence. I dare risk being sent to the Tower. It's time to speak. My services are quite forgotten.
QUEEN MARGARET.
[Aside.] Out, devil! I remember them only too well:
You killed my husband Henry in the Tower, and Edward, my poor son, at Tewkesbury.

RICHARD. Before you were queen, yes, or your husband king, I was a pack-horse in his great affairs — a weeder-out of his proud enemies, a generous rewarder of his friends. To make his blood royal, I spilled my own.
QUEEN MARGARET.
[Aside.] Yes, and far better blood than his or yours.

RICHARD. All that time, you and your husband Grey were partisans for the house of Lancaster. And, Rivers, so were you. Wasn't your husband killed in Margaret's battle at Saint Albans? Let me remind you, in case you've forgotten, what you used to be and what you are now — and also what I have been and what I am.
QUEEN MARGARET.
[Aside.] A murderous villain, and so you still are.
RICHARD. Poor Clarence abandoned his father Warwick — yes, and broke his oath, which may Jesus pardon! —
QUEEN MARGARET.
[Aside.] Which God avenge!

RICHARD. To fight on Edward's side for the crown. And as his reward, poor lord, he's locked up. I wish to God my heart were flint, like Edward's, or Edward's were soft and pitying, like mine. I am too childishly soft for this world.
QUEEN MARGARET.
[Aside.] Hurry off to hell for shame, and leave this world,
you cacodemon! Hell is your kingdom.
RIVERS. My lord of Gloucester, in those troubled days you bring up now to prove us your enemies, we were following then our lord, our sovereign king. So would we follow you, if you were our king.
RICHARD. If I should be! I'd rather be a peddler. Far be it from my heart even to think of it.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. As little joy, my lord, as you imagine you'd have if you were this country's king, that's how little joy you may suppose I have being its Queen.
QUEEN MARGARET.
[Aside.] As little joy as the Queen of it enjoys,
for I am she, and utterly joyless. I can't hold back any longer.
[Coming forward.]

Hear me, you squabbling pirates, falling out over what you've stolen from me! Which of you doesn't tremble when you look at me? If you don't bow like subjects because I'm Queen, you should still quake like rebels, because by you I've been deposed. Ah, gentle villain, don't turn away.
RICHARD. Foul wrinkled witch, what are you doing in my sight?
QUEEN MARGARET. Only repeating what you have ruined. That's what I'll do before I let you go.
RICHARD. Weren't you banished on pain of death?

QUEEN MARGARET. I was, but I find more pain in banishment than death can give me here by staying. You owe me a husband and a son. And you a kingdom; all of you, allegiance. This sorrow that is mine by right is yours. And all the pleasures you usurp are mine.

RICHARD. The curse my noble father laid on you, when you crowned his warlike brows with paper, and with your scorn drew rivers from his eyes, and then to dry them, gave the Duke a cloth steeped in the blameless blood of sweet Rutland — his curses then, from the bitterness of his soul, denounced against you, have all fallen on you. And God, not we, has plagued your bloody deed.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. So just is God, to right the innocent.
HASTINGS. Oh, it was the foulest deed to slay that babe, and the most merciless ever heard of.
RIVERS. Even tyrants wept when it was reported.
DORSET. Every man prophesied revenge for it.
BUCKINGHAM. Northumberland, who was there, wept to see it.

QUEEN MARGARET. What, were you all snarling at each other before I came, ready to grab one another by the throat — and now you turn all your hatred on me? Did York's dreadful curse have such power with heaven that Henry's death, my lovely Edward's death, the loss of their kingdom, my wretched banishment — should all just answer for that peevish brat? Can curses pierce the clouds and enter heaven? Why then, give way, dull clouds, to my quick curses! Though not by war, may your King die by overindulgence, as ours died by murder to make him a king. May Edward your son, who is now Prince of Wales, die young by similar untimely violence, just as Edward our son, who was Prince of Wales, did. May you yourself, a queen — in place of me who was a queen — outlive your glory, like my wretched self. May you live long to wail your children's deaths, and see another, as I see you now, decked in your rights, as you sit in mine. May your happy days die long before your death, and after many drawn-out hours of grief, may you die neither mother, wife, nor England's Queen. Rivers and Dorset, you were standing by, and so were you, Lord Hastings, when my son was stabbed with bloody daggers. God, I pray, that none of you may live out his natural age, but be cut off by some unforeseen accident.
RICHARD. Finish your spell, you hateful withered hag.

QUEEN MARGARET. And leave you out? Stay, dog, for you shall hear me. If heaven has any terrible plague in store beyond what I can wish on you, oh, let them save it until your sins are ripe, and then hurl their indignation down on you, the disturber of the poor world's peace. May the worm of conscience gnaw at your soul. May you suspect your friends as traitors while you live, and take deep traitors for your dearest friends. May no sleep close that deadly eye of yours, unless it's while some tormenting dream frightens you with a hell of ugly devils. You elvish-marked, abortive, rooting hog, you who at your birth were sealed as the slave of nature and the son of hell. You slander on your heavy mother's womb, you loathed product of your father's loins, you rag of honor, you detested —
RICHARD. Margaret.
QUEEN MARGARET. Richard!
RICHARD. Ha?
QUEEN MARGARET. I didn't call you.
RICHARD. I beg your pardon, then. I thought you'd called me all those bitter names.
QUEEN MARGARET. Why, so I did, but I expected no reply. Oh, let me finish my curse!
RICHARD. It's been finished by me, and ends in "Margaret."
QUEEN ELIZABETH. So you've breathed your curse against yourself.

QUEEN MARGARET. Poor painted queen, vain flourish of my fortune, why do you sprinkle sugar on that bottled spider, whose deadly web is closing around you? Fool, fool — you're whetting a knife to kill yourself. The day will come when you'll wish for me to help you curse this poisonous hunch-backed toad.
HASTINGS. False-foretelling woman, end your frantic curse, before you provoke our patience and harm yourself.
QUEEN MARGARET. Foul shame on you all — you have moved mine.
RIVERS. If you were properly served, you'd be taught your place.
QUEEN MARGARET. To serve me properly, you should all do me duty: teach me to be your queen, and you my subjects. Oh, serve me well, and teach yourselves that duty!
DORSET. Don't argue with her — she's mad.

QUEEN MARGARET. Quiet, Master Marquess, you're impertinent. Your brand-new badge of honor is hardly current. Oh, if only your young nobility could understand what it would be to lose it and be miserable. Those who stand high have many gusts to shake them, and if they fall they dash themselves to pieces.
RICHARD. Good advice, truly. Learn it, learn it, Marquess.
DORSET. It concerns you, my lord, as much as me.
RICHARD. Yes, and much more. But I was born high. Our eyrie nests in the cedar's top, and toys with the wind, and scorns the sun.

QUEEN MARGARET. And turns the sun to shadow, alas, alas! Witness my son, now in the shadow of death, whose bright outshining beams your cloudy wrath has folded up in eternal darkness. Your eyrie nests in our eyrie's nest. O God, you who see it, do not allow it! As it was won with blood, may it be lost the same way.
BUCKINGHAM. Peace, peace, for shame, if not for charity.

QUEEN MARGARET. Don't urge charity or shame on me. You have dealt with me uncharitably, and shamefully my hopes have been butchered by you. My charity is outrage, my life is shame, and in that shame my sorrow's rage lives on.
BUCKINGHAM. Stop, stop.

QUEEN MARGARET. O princely Buckingham, I'll kiss your hand as a sign of league and friendship with you. May good fortune attend you and your noble house! Your garments are not spotted with our blood, nor are you within the compass of my curse.
BUCKINGHAM. Nor is anyone here, since curses never pass beyond the lips of those who breathe them into the air.

QUEEN MARGARET. I'll believe rather that they rise to the sky and there wake God's gentle sleeping peace. O Buckingham, watch out for that dog over there! Look — when he fawns, he bites. And when he bites, his venomous tooth will fester until death. Have nothing to do with him. Beware of him. Sin, death, and hell have set their marks on him, and all their ministers attend on him.
RICHARD. What is she saying, my lord of Buckingham?
BUCKINGHAM. Nothing I take seriously, my gracious lord.

QUEEN MARGARET. What, do you scorn me for my gentle counsel, and flatter the devil I warn you against? Oh, but remember this another day, when he splits your very heart with sorrow, and you say, poor Margaret was a prophetess. May each of you live as subjects to his hate, and he to yours, and all of you to God's!
[Exit.]
BUCKINGHAM. My hair stands on end to hear her curses.
RIVERS. So does mine. I wonder why she's at liberty.
RICHARD. I can't blame her. By God's holy mother, she has had too much wrong done to her, and I repent my part in what I have done to her.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. I never did her any wrong, as far as I know.

RICHARD. Yet you have all the advantage of her wrong. I was too quick to do good for somebody who is now too cold in thinking of it. As for Clarence, he's well rewarded — he's penned up to be fattened for his pains. God pardon those who are the cause of it.
RIVERS. A virtuous and Christian-like conclusion, to pray for those who have done us harm.
RICHARD. So I always do — (speaks to himself) being well advised; for if I had cursed now, I would have cursed myself.
[Enter CATESBY.]
CATESBY. Madam, His Majesty calls for you, and for Your Grace, and you, my gracious lords.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Catesby, I'm coming. Lords, will you go with me?
RIVERS. We attend on Your Grace.
[Exeunt all but RICHARD.]

RICHARD. I do the wrong, and I'm the first to start the quarrel. The secret mischiefs I set in motion I lay as a grievous charge on others. Clarence, whom I have indeed cast into darkness, I weep for in front of many simple fools — namely, Derby, Hastings, Buckingham — and tell them it's the Queen and her allies who stir the King against my brother the Duke. Now they believe it, and on top of that they spur me on to be revenged on Rivers, Dorset, Grey. But then I sigh, and with a piece of Scripture, tell them that God commands us to do good for evil. And so I clothe my naked villainy with odd old scraps stolen from Holy Writ, and seem a saint when I most play the devil.
[Enter two MURDERERS.]
But soft, here come my executioners. How now, my hardy, stout, resolved mates — are you going to dispatch this matter now?
FIRST MURDERER. We are, my lord, and have come to get the warrant, so we can be admitted where he is.
RICHARD. Well thought of. I have it here.
[Gives the warrant.]

When you have done it, come to Crosby Place. But, sirs, be quick in the execution, and obstinate too — don't listen to him plead. For Clarence is well-spoken, and may move your hearts to pity if you pay attention to him.
SECOND MURDERER. Tut, tut, my lord, we won't stop to chatter. Talkers are no good doers. Rest assured, we go to use our hands, not our tongues.
RICHARD. Your eyes drop millstones when fools' eyes drop tears. I like you, lads. About your business at once. Go, go, dispatch.
BOTH MURDERERS. We will, my noble lord.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 4 — London. A Room in the Tower
paragraphs: [Enter CLARENCE and a KEEPER.]
KEEPER. Why does Your Grace look so heavy-hearted today?

CLARENCE. Oh, I have spent a miserable night, so full of fearful dreams, of ugly sights, that — as I am a Christian faithful man — I would not spend another such a night even to buy a world of happy days, so full of dismal terror was the time!
KEEPER. What was your dream, my lord? Please tell me.

CLARENCE. I thought that I had broken out of the Tower, and was on board a ship to cross to Burgundy. And in my company was my brother Gloucester, who tempted me from my cabin to walk up on the hatches. From there we looked toward England, and recalled a thousand grim moments, during the wars of York and Lancaster, that had happened to us. As we paced along on the unsteady footing of the hatches, I thought Gloucester stumbled, and in falling, struck me — who tried to steady him — overboard into the tumbling waves of the open sea. Oh Lord, I thought, what pain it was to drown, what dreadful noise of waters in my ears, what sights of ugly death within my eyes! I thought I saw a thousand fearful shipwrecks, a thousand men whom fish gnawed on, wedges of gold, great anchors, heaps of pearl, priceless stones, beyond-price jewels, all scattered on the bottom of the sea. Some lay in dead men's skulls, and in the holes where eyes once had been, there had crept — as if in mockery of eyes — reflecting gems, that wooed the slimy bottom of the deep, and mocked the dead bones lying scattered nearby.
KEEPER. Did you have such leisure at the moment of death to gaze upon these secrets of the deep?

CLARENCE. I thought I did. And often I tried to give up the ghost, but the envious flood stopped my soul, and would not let it out to find the empty, vast, wandering air. Instead it smothered it within my panting body, which almost burst trying to belch it into the sea.
KEEPER. Didn't you wake in this sore agony?

CLARENCE. No, no — my dream went on after death. Oh, then the real tempest came over my soul. I crossed, I thought, the melancholy river, with that sour ferryman the poets write about, into the kingdom of perpetual night. The first to greet my stranger-soul there was my great father-in-law, renowned Warwick, who cried aloud, "What scourge for perjury can this dark monarchy provide for false Clarence?" And so he vanished. Then there came drifting by a shadow like an angel, with bright hair dabbled in blood. And he shrieked out loud, "Clarence is come — false, fleeting, perjured Clarence, who stabbed me in the field at Tewkesbury! Seize him, Furies! Take him to torment!" With that, I thought, a legion of foul fiends surrounded me, and howled in my ears such hideous cries that with the very noise I awoke trembling, and for some time afterward could not believe but that I was in hell — such terrible impression my dream made.
KEEPER. No wonder, my lord, that it frightened you. I'm afraid even to hear you tell it.

CLARENCE. Ah, Keeper, Keeper, I have done these things, which now testify against my soul, for Edward's sake — and see how he rewards me. O God, if my deep prayers can't appease you, but you will be avenged on my misdeeds, yet execute your wrath on me alone. Oh, spare my innocent wife and my poor children! Keeper, please sit by me a while. My soul is heavy, and I'd like to sleep.
KEEPER. I will, my lord. God give Your Grace good rest.
[CLARENCE settles down on a chair.]
[Enter BRAKENBURY the Lieutenant.]

BRAKENBURY. Sorrow disrupts seasons and resting hours, makes night into morning, and noontime into night. Princes have only their titles for their glory, an outward honor for an inward labor. And, for unfelt fantasies, they often feel a world of restless cares. So that between their titles and a common name, the only difference is the outward fame.
[Enter the two MURDERERS.]
FIRST MURDERER. Ho, who's there?
BRAKENBURY. What do you want, fellow? And how did you get here?
SECOND MURDERER. I want to speak with Clarence, and I came here on my legs.
BRAKENBURY. What, so curt?
FIRST MURDERER. It's better, sir, than being long-winded. Let him see our commission, and don't talk any more.
[BRAKENBURY reads the commission.]

BRAKENBURY. I am ordered by this to deliver the noble Duke of Clarence into your hands. I won't reason about what's meant by it, because I want to be guiltless of the meaning. There the Duke lies asleep, and there the keys. I'll go to the King and let him know that I have thus resigned my charge to you.
FIRST MURDERER. You may, sir. It's a point of wisdom. Farewell.
[Exeunt BRAKENBURY and the KEEPER.]
SECOND MURDERER. What, shall I stab him while he sleeps?
FIRST MURDERER. No. He'll say we did it cowardly, when he wakes.
SECOND MURDERER. Why, he'll never wake until the great Judgment Day.
FIRST MURDERER. Why then, he'll say we stabbed him while sleeping.
SECOND MURDERER. The mention of that word "judgment" has bred a kind of remorse in me.
FIRST MURDERER. What, are you afraid?
SECOND MURDERER. Not to kill him — I have a warrant — but to be damned for killing him, which no warrant can protect me from.
FIRST MURDERER. I thought you were resolute.
SECOND MURDERER. So I am — resolute to let him live.
FIRST MURDERER. I'll go back to the Duke of Gloucester and tell him so.
SECOND MURDERER. No, please wait a little. I hope this passionate mood will change. It usually only lasts as long as it takes to count to twenty.
FIRST MURDERER. How do you feel now?
SECOND MURDERER. Honestly, some leftover dregs of conscience are still in me.
FIRST MURDERER. Remember our reward, when the deed's done.
SECOND MURDERER. By God's wounds, he dies! I had forgotten the reward.
FIRST MURDERER. Where's your conscience now?
SECOND MURDERER. Oh, in the Duke of Gloucester's purse.
FIRST MURDERER. So, when he opens his purse to give us our reward, your conscience flies out.
SECOND MURDERER. No matter, let it go. Few or none will take it in.
FIRST MURDERER. What if it comes back to you?

SECOND MURDERER. I won't bother with it. It makes a man a coward. A man can't steal but it accuses him. A man can't swear but it checks him. A man can't sleep with his neighbor's wife but it gives him away. It's a blushing, shamefaced spirit that mutinies in a man's chest. It fills a man with obstacles. It once made me return a purse of gold that I'd found by chance. It beggars any man who keeps it. It is driven out of towns and cities as a dangerous thing. And every man who means to live well tries to trust to himself and live without it.
FIRST MURDERER. By God's wounds, it's right here at my elbow now, persuading me not to kill the Duke.
SECOND MURDERER. Take the devil into your mind, and don't believe him. He would worm in on you only to make you sigh.
FIRST MURDERER. I'm strong-framed — he can't prevail with me.
SECOND MURDERER. Spoken like a tall man who respects his reputation. Come, shall we get to work?
FIRST MURDERER. Hit him on the head with the hilt of your sword, and then throw him into the malmsey cask in the next room.
SECOND MURDERER. Oh, excellent idea — and make a sop of him.
FIRST MURDERER. Soft, he's waking.
SECOND MURDERER. Strike!
FIRST MURDERER. No, we'll reason with him.
CLARENCE. Where are you, Keeper? Give me a cup of wine.
SECOND MURDERER. You'll have wine enough, my lord, before long.
CLARENCE. In God's name, what are you?
FIRST MURDERER. A man, as you are.
CLARENCE. But not, as I am, royal.
SECOND MURDERER. Nor you, as we are, loyal.
CLARENCE. Your voice is thunder, but your looks are humble.
FIRST MURDERER. My voice is now the King's, my looks are my own.
CLARENCE. How darkly and how deadly you speak! Your eyes threaten me. Why do you look pale? Who sent you here? Why do you come?
SECOND MURDERER. To, to, to —
CLARENCE. To murder me?
BOTH MURDERERS. Yes, yes.
CLARENCE. You scarcely have the hearts to tell me so, and therefore can't have the hearts to do it. In what way, my friends, have I offended you?
FIRST MURDERER. You haven't offended us, but the King.
CLARENCE. I shall be reconciled to him again.
SECOND MURDERER. Never, my lord. Therefore prepare to die.

CLARENCE. Are you chosen out of a whole world of men to slay the innocent? What is my offense? Where is the evidence that accuses me? What lawful inquest has given its verdict to the frowning judge? Or who pronounced the bitter sentence of poor Clarence's death? Before I am convicted by due process of law, to threaten me with death is most unlawful. I charge you, as you hope for redemption by Christ's dear blood shed for our grievous sins, to depart and lay no hands on me. The deed you undertake is damnable.
FIRST MURDERER. What we will do, we do on orders.
SECOND MURDERER. And he who has given the orders is our King.

CLARENCE. Misguided servants! The great King of kings has commanded in the tablet of his law that you shall not commit murder. Will you then spurn his edict and fulfill a man's? Take care, for he holds vengeance in his hand to hurl upon the heads of those who break his law.
SECOND MURDERER. And that same vengeance he hurls on you — for false swearing, and for murder too. You received the sacrament to fight in the quarrel of the house of Lancaster.
FIRST MURDERER. And like a traitor to the name of God, you broke that vow, and with your treacherous blade ripped open the bowels of your sovereign's son.
SECOND MURDERER. Whom you were sworn to cherish and defend.
FIRST MURDERER. How can you urge God's dreadful law on us, when you have broken it to such a deep degree?

CLARENCE. Alas — for whose sake did I do that ill deed? For Edward, for my brother, for his sake. He doesn't send you to murder me for this, for in that sin he is as deep as I am. If God will be avenged for the deed, oh, know that he does it publicly. Don't take the quarrel from his powerful arm. He needs no indirect or lawless way to cut off those who have offended him.
FIRST MURDERER. Who made you then a bloody minister, when gallant, spring-fresh, brave Plantagenet — that princely novice — was struck dead by you?
CLARENCE. My brother's love, the devil, and my rage.
FIRST MURDERER. Your brother's love, our duty, and your own faults, prompt us here now to slaughter you.

CLARENCE. If you love my brother, don't hate me. I am his brother, and I love him well. If you're hired for pay, go back, and I'll send you to my brother Gloucester, who'll reward you better for my life than Edward will for news of my death.
SECOND MURDERER. You are deceived. Your brother Gloucester hates you.
CLARENCE. Oh no, he loves me, and he holds me dear. Go to him from me.
FIRST MURDERER. Yes, so we will.

CLARENCE. Tell him that when our princely father York blessed his three sons with his victorious arm, and charged us, from his soul, to love each other, he little thought of this divided friendship. Tell Gloucester to think of this, and he will weep.
FIRST MURDERER. Yes, millstones — as he taught us to weep.
CLARENCE. Oh, don't slander him, for he is kind.
FIRST MURDERER. Right — as snow in harvest. Come, you're deceiving yourself. It's he who sends us to destroy you here.
CLARENCE. It can't be, for he wept over my fortune, and hugged me in his arms, and swore with sobs that he would work for my release.
FIRST MURDERER. Why, so he does — when he delivers you from this earth's thrall into the joys of heaven.
SECOND MURDERER. Make your peace with God, for you must die, my lord.

CLARENCE. Do you have that holy feeling in your souls to counsel me to make my peace with God, and yet are you so blind to your own souls that you'll war with God by murdering me? Oh, sirs, consider: those who set you to this deed will hate you for the deed.
SECOND MURDERER. What shall we do?
CLARENCE. Relent, and save your souls.
FIRST MURDERER. Relent? No, that's cowardly and womanish.

CLARENCE. Not to relent is beastly, savage, devilish. Which of you — if you were a prince's son, locked away from liberty as I am now — if two such murderers as yourselves came to you, would not plead for life? Yes, you would beg, were you in my distress. My friend, I see some pity in your looks. Oh, if your eye is no flatterer, come to my side, and plead for me. What beggar doesn't pity a begging prince?
SECOND MURDERER. Look behind you, my lord.
FIRST MURDERER. Take that, and that! [Stabs him.] If all this won't do it, I'll drown you in the malmsey cask in the next room.
[Exit with the body.]
SECOND MURDERER. A bloody deed, and desperately carried out. How gladly, like Pilate, I would wash my hands of this most grievous murder.
[Enter FIRST MURDERER.]
FIRST MURDERER. What's this? What do you mean by not helping me? By heaven, the Duke shall know how slack you've been.
SECOND MURDERER. I wish he knew that I had saved his brother. Take the fee yourself, and tell him what I say — for I repent that the Duke is slain.
[Exit.]

FIRST MURDERER. So do not I. Go, coward as you are. Well, I'll go hide the body in some hole until the Duke gives orders for his burial. And when I have my pay, I'll be off — for this will come out, and then I mustn't stay.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 1 — London. A Room in the palace
paragraphs: [Enter KING EDWARD, sick, QUEEN ELIZABETH, DORSET, RIVERS, HASTINGS, BUCKINGHAM, GREY, and others.]

KING EDWARD. Well, there. Now I've done a good day's work. You peers, keep this united alliance going. Every day I expect a summons from my Redeemer, to redeem me away from here. And my soul shall depart to heaven more at peace, since I've made my friends at peace on earth. Rivers and Hastings, take each other's hand. Don't disguise your hatred — swear your love.
RIVERS. By heaven, my soul is purged of all grudging hate, and with my hand I seal my true heart's love.
HASTINGS. So may I thrive, as I truly swear the same.
KING EDWARD. Take care you don't trifle in your King's presence, lest he who is the supreme King of kings confound your hidden falsehood, and arrange that one of you be the other's death.
HASTINGS. So may I prosper, as I swear perfect love.
RIVERS. And I, as I love Hastings with my heart.

KING EDWARD. Madam, you yourself aren't exempt from this — nor you, son Dorset; Buckingham, nor you. You have all been factious against each other. Wife, love Lord Hastings; let him kiss your hand. And whatever you do, do it without pretense.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. There, Hastings — I'll never remember our former hatred again, so may I and mine thrive.
KING EDWARD. Dorset, embrace him. Hastings, love the lord Marquess.
DORSET. This exchange of love, I declare here, shall on my part be inviolable.
HASTINGS. And so I swear.
[They embrace.]
KING EDWARD. Now, princely Buckingham, seal this league with your embrace of my wife's relations, and make me happy in your unity.

BUCKINGHAM. Whenever Buckingham turns his hate on Your Grace — instead of cherishing you and yours with all dutiful love — may God punish me with hate from those where I expect most love. When I most need to call on a friend, and am most certain that he is a friend, may he prove deep, hollow, treacherous, and full of guile to me: this I beg of God, if I am ever cold in love to you or yours.
[Embrace.]
KING EDWARD. A pleasing cordial, princely Buckingham, is this vow to my sickly heart. We only lack our brother Gloucester here, to make the blessed completion of this peace.
BUCKINGHAM. And in good time — here come Sir Ratcliffe and the Duke.
[Enter RATCLIFFE and RICHARD.]
RICHARD. Good morning to my sovereign King and Queen, and to you, princely peers, a happy time of day.
KING EDWARD. Happy indeed, as we have spent the day. Gloucester, we've done deeds of charity — made peace out of enmity, fair love out of hate, between these swelling, wrong-stirred peers.

RICHARD. A blessed labor, my most sovereign lord. Among this princely company, if anyone here, by false report or wrong assumption, holds me an enemy — if I unwittingly, or in my rage, have done anything that any in this company finds hard to bear — I desire to reconcile myself to his friendly peace. It is death to me to be at enmity. I hate it, and desire all good men's love. First, madam, I beg true peace of you, which I will purchase with my dutiful service. Of you, my noble cousin Buckingham, if any grudge has ever lodged between us. Of you, and you, Lord Rivers and Dorset, who have all without cause frowned on me. Of you, Lord Woodville and Lord Scales; of you, dukes, earls, lords, gentlemen — indeed, of all. I don't know an Englishman alive with whom my soul is one bit at odds, any more than the infant born tonight. I thank my God for my humility.

QUEEN ELIZABETH. May this day be kept as a holy day from now on. I wish to God all quarrels were well settled. My sovereign lord, I beg Your Highness to take our brother Clarence back into your grace.
RICHARD. Why, madam, have I offered love for this, to be so mocked in this royal presence? Who doesn't know that the gentle Duke is dead?
[They all start.]
You do him an injury, scorning his corpse.
KING EDWARD. Who doesn't know he's dead? Who knows that he is?
QUEEN ELIZABETH. All-seeing heaven, what a world this is!
BUCKINGHAM. Do I look as pale, Lord Dorset, as the rest?
DORSET. Yes, my good lord, and no man in this company hasn't lost his red color from his cheeks.
KING EDWARD. Is Clarence dead? The order was reversed.

RICHARD. But he, poor man, died by your first order — which a winged Mercury delivered. Some tardy cripple carried the counter-order, but came too late to see him buried. God grant that some others — less noble and less loyal, nearer in bloody thoughts though not in blood — don't deserve worse than wretched Clarence did, and yet escape suspicion!
[Enter STANLEY, Earl of Derby.]
STANLEY. A boon, my sovereign, for service done!
KING EDWARD. Please, peace. My soul is full of sorrow.
STANLEY. I won't rise unless Your Highness hears me.
KING EDWARD. Then say at once what it is you ask.
STANLEY. The forfeit, sovereign, of my servant's life — who today killed a riotous gentleman lately attending on the Duke of Norfolk.

KING EDWARD. Do I have a tongue to doom my brother's death, and shall that tongue give pardon to a slave? My brother killed no man — his fault was a thought, and yet his punishment was bitter death. Who pleaded to me for him? Who, in my wrath, knelt at my feet and bid me reconsider? Who spoke of brotherhood? Who spoke of love? Who told me how the poor soul forsook the mighty Warwick, and fought for me? Who told me, in the field at Tewkesbury, when Oxford had me down, that he rescued me, and said, "Dear brother, live, and be a king"? Who told me, when we both lay in the field nearly frozen to death, how he wrapped me even in his garments, and gave himself, all thin and naked, to the numb-cold night? All this brutish wrath sinfully plucked from my remembrance, and not a man of you had so much grace as to put it back in my mind. But when your carters or your waiting servants have done a drunken slaughter, and disfigured the precious image of our dear Redeemer, you are straight on your knees for pardon, pardon — and I, unjustly too, must grant it you. But for my brother not a man would speak, nor would I — ungrateful — speak to myself for him, poor soul. The proudest of you all has been beholden to him in his life, yet none of you would once beg for his life. O God, I fear your justice will take hold on me, and on you, and on mine and yours for this! Come, Hastings, help me to my private chamber. Ah, poor Clarence!
[Exeunt some with KING and QUEEN.]

RICHARD. This is the fruit of rashness. Did you notice how the guilty kindred of the Queen looked pale when they heard of Clarence's death? Oh, they kept urging it to the King. God will avenge it. Come, lords, will you go to comfort Edward with our company?
BUCKINGHAM. We attend on Your Grace.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 2 — Another Room in the palace
paragraphs: [Enter the old DUCHESS OF YORK with the two CHILDREN of Clarence.]
BOY. Good grandmother, tell us — is our father dead?
DUCHESS. No, boy.
GIRL. Why do you weep so often, and beat your breast, and cry, "Oh Clarence, my unhappy son"?
BOY. Why do you look on us, and shake your head, and call us orphans, wretches, castaways, if our noble father were alive?
DUCHESS. My pretty cousins, you've both misread me. I mourn the sickness of the King, hating to lose him — not your father's death. It would be wasted sorrow to wail for one who's already lost.
BOY. Then by that, grandmother, you confirm he is dead. The King my uncle is to blame. God will avenge it, and I'll press him with earnest prayers all to that effect.
GIRL. And so will I.
DUCHESS. Peace, children, peace. The King loves you well. Slow and shallow innocents — you can't guess who caused your father's death.

BOY. Grandmother, we can — for my good uncle Gloucester told me the King, provoked to it by the Queen, devised impeachments to imprison him. And when my uncle told me so, he wept, and pitied me, and kindly kissed my cheek. He told me to rely on him as on my father, and that he would love me dearly as his own child.
DUCHESS. Ah, that deceit should steal such a gentle shape, and with a virtuous mask hide deep vice! He is my son, yes, and there is my shame — yet he did not draw this deceit from my breast.
BOY. Do you think my uncle was lying, grandmother?
DUCHESS. Yes, boy.
BOY. I can't think it. Listen, what noise is that?
[Enter QUEEN ELIZABETH with her hair about her ears, RIVERS and DORSET after her.]
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Ah, who shall stop me from wailing and weeping, from cursing my fortune, and tormenting myself? I'll join with black despair against my soul, and become an enemy to myself.
DUCHESS. What does this scene of rude impatience mean?

QUEEN ELIZABETH. An act of tragic violence. Edward, my lord, your son, our King, is dead. Why do the branches grow when the root is gone? Why don't the leaves wither when their sap is gone? If you will live, lament. If die, be brief, so that our swift-winged souls may catch the King's — or, like obedient subjects, follow him to his new kingdom of never-changing night.

DUCHESS. Ah, I have as much claim in your sorrow as I had title in your noble husband. I have wept the death of a worthy husband, and lived by looking on his images. But now two mirrors of his princely likeness are shattered in pieces by malignant death, and I, for comfort, have only one false mirror, which grieves me when I see my shame in him. You are a widow, yet you are a mother, and have the comfort of your children left. But death has snatched my husband from my arms, and plucked two crutches from my feeble hands — Clarence and Edward. Oh, what cause have I — yours being only a part of my grief — to outdo your woes and drown your cries.
BOY. Ah, aunt, you didn't weep for our father's death. How can we help you with our family tears?
GIRL. Our fatherless distress was left unmourned. May your widow-grief likewise be unwept!

QUEEN ELIZABETH. Give me no help in lamentation. I'm not barren in bringing forth complaints. Let all springs reduce their currents to my eyes, so that I, being governed by the watery moon, may send forth plenteous tears to drown the world. Ah, for my husband, for my dear Lord Edward!
CHILDREN. Ah, for our father, for our dear Lord Clarence!
DUCHESS. Alas, for both — both mine, Edward and Clarence!
QUEEN ELIZABETH. What support had I but Edward? And he's gone.
CHILDREN. What support had we but Clarence? And he's gone.
DUCHESS. What supports had I but they? And they are gone.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Never was a widow with so dear a loss.
CHILDREN. Never were orphans with so dear a loss.

DUCHESS. Never was a mother with so dear a loss. Alas, I am the mother of these griefs. Their woes are partial; mine is general. She weeps for an Edward, and so do I. I weep for a Clarence, but she does not. These babes weep for Clarence, and so do I. I weep for an Edward, but they do not. Alas, you three, on me, threefold distressed, pour out all your tears. I am your sorrow's nurse, and I will pamper it with lamentation.

DORSET. Comfort, dear mother. God is much displeased that you take his doings with ungratefulness. In common worldly things it's called ungrateful to repay reluctantly a debt that was kindly lent with a bounteous hand. Much more so to be thus contrary with heaven, for it asks back the royal debt it lent you.

RIVERS. Madam, think, like a careful mother, of the young prince your son. Send for him at once. Let him be crowned. In him your comfort lives. Drown desperate sorrow in dead Edward's grave, and plant your joys in living Edward's throne.
[Enter RICHARD, BUCKINGHAM, STANLEY Earl of Derby, HASTINGS, and RATCLIFFE.]

RICHARD. Sister, take comfort. All of us have cause to wail the dimming of our shining star, but none can help our harms by wailing them. Madam my mother, I beg your pardon — I didn't see Your Grace. Humbly on my knee I ask your blessing.
[Kneels.]
DUCHESS. God bless you, and put meekness into your breast — love, charity, obedience, and true duty.
RICHARD. Amen. [Aside.] And make me die a good old man! That's the proper ending of a mother's blessing — I'm amazed Her Grace left it out.

BUCKINGHAM. You cloudy princes and heart-sorrowing peers who carry this heavy mutual load of mourning, now cheer each other in each other's love. Though we've spent our harvest of this king, we're to reap the harvest of his son. The broken rancor of your high-swollen hates, only lately mended, knitted, and joined together, must be gently preserved, cherished, and kept. It seems good to me that with a small retinue, the young Prince be brought without delay from Ludlow here to London, to be crowned our King.
RIVERS. Why with a small retinue, my Lord of Buckingham?

BUCKINGHAM. Truly, my lord, lest with a multitude the newly healed wound of malice should break out — which would be the more dangerous because the realm is so green and ungoverned. Where every horse holds its commanding rein and may direct its course as it pleases, the fear of harm — as well as harm itself — should, in my opinion, be prevented.
RICHARD. I hope the King made peace with all of us, and the compact is firm and true in me.

RIVERS. And so in me, and, I think, in all. Yet since it's only just made, it shouldn't be put under any apparent likelihood of breach — which might happen with too much company. So I say, with noble Buckingham, that it's fitting only a few should fetch the Prince.
HASTINGS. And so say I.
RICHARD. Then so be it, and let's go decide who they shall be that will post immediately to Ludlow. Madam, and you, my sister, will you go to give your opinions on this business?
[Exeunt all but BUCKINGHAM and RICHARD.]

BUCKINGHAM. My lord, whoever journeys to the Prince, for God's sake, don't let us two stay home. For on the way I'll find the chance, as a starting point for the story we lately talked of, to part the Queen's proud kindred from the Prince.
RICHARD. My other self, my counsel's chamber, my oracle, my prophet, my dear cousin — I, like a child, will go by your direction. Toward Ludlow then, for we won't stay behind.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 3 — London. A street
paragraphs: [Enter one CITIZEN at one door, and another at the other.]
FIRST CITIZEN. Good morning, neighbor — where are you off to so fast?
SECOND CITIZEN. I assure you, I scarcely know myself. Have you heard the news?
FIRST CITIZEN. Yes — that the King is dead.
SECOND CITIZEN. Bad news, by our Lady; the better seldom comes. I fear it will turn out to be a giddy, unsettled world.
[Enter another CITIZEN.]
THIRD CITIZEN. Good day, neighbors.
FIRST CITIZEN. Good morning to you, sir.
THIRD CITIZEN. Is the news of good King Edward's death confirmed?
SECOND CITIZEN. Yes, sir, it's all too true — God help us in the meantime.
THIRD CITIZEN. Then, gentlemen, expect a troubled world.
FIRST CITIZEN. No, no — by God's good grace, his son shall reign.
THIRD CITIZEN. Woe to that land that's governed by a child.

SECOND CITIZEN. In him there's a hope of government — which, in his minority, the council will run under him, and, in his full and ripened years, he himself shall, no doubt, both then and till then, govern well.
FIRST CITIZEN. The state was in the same condition when Henry the Sixth was crowned in Paris at only nine months old.
THIRD CITIZEN. Was the state the same? No, no, good friends, God knows. For then this land was famously enriched with sound, grave counsel. Then the King had virtuous uncles to protect his Grace.
FIRST CITIZEN. Why, so has this one — both on his father's side and his mother's.

THIRD CITIZEN. It would be better if they all came on his father's side, or that there were none at all on his father's side, for the rivalry over who shall now be closest will touch us all too closely, if God doesn't prevent it. Oh, the Duke of Gloucester is full of danger, and the Queen's sons and brothers are haughty and proud. If they were to be ruled, not to rule, this sickly land might find comfort as before.
FIRST CITIZEN. Come, come — we fear the worst; all will be well.

THIRD CITIZEN. When clouds appear, wise men put on their cloaks. When great leaves fall, winter is at hand. When the sun sets, who doesn't look for night? Untimely storms make men expect a famine. All may be well — but if God arranges it so, it's more than we deserve or I expect.
SECOND CITIZEN. Truly, men's hearts are full of fear. You can scarcely reason with a man who doesn't look heavy and full of dread.

THIRD CITIZEN. Before days of change, it's always so. By a divine instinct men's minds mistrust the coming danger — as we see by proof that the water swells before a boisterous storm. But leave it all to God. Where are you off to?
SECOND CITIZEN. Truly, we were sent for to the Justices.
THIRD CITIZEN. And so was I. I'll come along with you.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 4 — London. A Room in the Palace
paragraphs: [Enter the ARCHBISHOP OF YORK, the young DUKE OF YORK, QUEEN ELIZABETH, and the DUCHESS OF YORK.]
ARCHBISHOP. Last night, I hear, they stayed at Stony Stratford, and tonight they rest at Northampton. Tomorrow or the next day they'll be here.
DUCHESS. I long with all my heart to see the Prince. I hope he's grown a lot since I last saw him.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. But I hear not. They say my son of York has almost overtaken him in his growth.
YORK. Yes, mother, but I wouldn't have it that way.
DUCHESS. Why, my good cousin? It's good to grow.

YORK. Grandmother, one night as we sat at supper, my uncle Rivers talked about how I was growing more than my brother. "Yes," said my uncle Gloucester, "small herbs have grace; great weeds grow apace." And since then, I think I wouldn't want to grow so fast, because sweet flowers are slow and weeds make haste.

DUCHESS. Good faith, good faith, the saying didn't hold in the one who applied it to you! He was the wretchedest thing when he was young, so long growing, and so slowly, that if his rule were true, he should be gracious.
ARCHBISHOP. And so, no doubt, he is, my gracious madam.
DUCHESS. I hope he is, but yet let mothers doubt.
YORK. Now, by my faith, if I had remembered, I could have given my uncle's Grace a quip to touch his growth nearer than he touched mine.
DUCHESS. How so, my young York? Please let me hear it.
YORK. Truly, they say my uncle grew so fast that he could gnaw a crust at two hours old. It was a full two years before I could get a tooth. Grandmother, this would have been a biting jest.
DUCHESS. Please, pretty York — who told you this?
YORK. Grandmother, his nurse.
DUCHESS. His nurse? Why, she was dead before you were born.
YORK. If it wasn't her, I can't tell who told me.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. A dangerous boy! Come now, you're too sharp.
DUCHESS. Good madam, don't be angry with the child.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Pitchers have ears.
[Enter a MESSENGER.]
ARCHBISHOP. Here comes a messenger. What news?
MESSENGER. Such news, my lord, as grieves me to report.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. How is the Prince?
MESSENGER. Well, madam, and in good health.
DUCHESS. What is your news?
MESSENGER. Lord Rivers and Lord Grey have been sent to Pomfret, and with them Sir Thomas Vaughan, as prisoners.
DUCHESS. Who has committed them?
MESSENGER. The mighty Dukes, Gloucester and Buckingham.
ARCHBISHOP. For what offense?
MESSENGER. The sum of all I can tell, I have disclosed. Why or for what the nobles were committed is all unknown to me, my gracious lord.

QUEEN ELIZABETH. Ah me! I see the ruin of my house. The tiger has now seized the gentle hind; insulting tyranny begins to jut over the innocent and undefended throne. Welcome, destruction, blood, and massacre — I see, as on a map, the end of it all.

DUCHESS. Accursed and unquiet wrangling days, how many of you have my eyes seen? My husband lost his life to gain the crown, and often my sons were tossed up and down, for me to rejoice and weep at their gains and losses. And once they were settled, and domestic strife clean blown over, they themselves — the conquerors — make war on themselves, brother to brother, blood to blood, self against self. Oh, preposterous and frantic outrage, end your damned spleen, or let me die, to look on earth no more.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Come, come, my boy. We'll go to sanctuary. Madam, farewell.
DUCHESS. Wait — I'll go with you.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. You have no cause.
ARCHBISHOP.
[To the QUEEN.] My gracious lady, go,

and take your treasure and your goods there. For my part, I'll resign to Your Grace the seal I keep; and so may it go with me as I show care for you and all of yours. Go — I'll escort you to sanctuary.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 1 — London. A street
paragraphs: [Trumpets sound. Enter young PRINCE EDWARD, RICHARD, BUCKINGHAM, CARDINAL BOURCHIER, CATESBY and others.]
BUCKINGHAM. Welcome, sweet Prince, to London, to your chamber.
RICHARD. Welcome, dear cousin, my thoughts' sovereign. The weary road has made you melancholy.
PRINCE. No, uncle — but our troubles on the way have made it tedious, wearisome, and heavy. I want more uncles here to welcome me.

RICHARD. Sweet prince, the untainted virtue of your years has not yet dived into the world's deceit. You can't distinguish a man any further than his outward show — which, God knows, seldom or never matches the heart. Those uncles you want were dangerous. Your Grace listened to their sugared words but didn't look at the poison in their hearts. God keep you from them, and from such false friends!
PRINCE. God keep me from false friends — but they weren't any.
RICHARD. My lord, the Mayor of London comes to greet you.
[Enter the LORD MAYOR with attendants.]
MAYOR. God bless Your Grace with health and happy days!

PRINCE. I thank you, good my lord, and thank you all. I thought my mother and my brother York would long before this have met us on the way. For shame — what a slug Hastings is, that he doesn't come to tell us whether they'll come or not!
[Enter LORD HASTINGS.]
BUCKINGHAM. And in good time, here comes the sweating lord.
PRINCE. Welcome, my lord. What — will our mother come?

HASTINGS. For what reason, God knows, not I — the Queen your mother and your brother York have taken sanctuary. The tender prince would gladly have come with me to meet Your Grace, but was forcibly held back by his mother.

BUCKINGHAM. For shame — what an indirect and peevish course this is of hers. Lord Cardinal, will Your Grace persuade the Queen to send the Duke of York to his princely brother right away? If she refuses, Lord Hastings, go with him, and from her jealous arms pluck him by force.

CARDINAL. My Lord of Buckingham, if my weak oratory can win the Duke of York from his mother, expect him here soon. But if she's obdurate to mild entreaties, God in heaven forbid that we should infringe the holy privilege of blessed sanctuary! Not for all this land would I be guilty of so deep a sin.

BUCKINGHAM. You are too unfeelingly stubborn, my lord, too ceremonious and traditional. Weigh it against the grossness of this age — you don't break sanctuary by seizing him. The benefit of sanctuary is always granted to those whose dealings have deserved the place, and those who have the wit to claim it. This prince has neither claimed it nor deserved it, and therefore, in my opinion, can't have it. Then in taking him from a place he isn't in, you break no privilege or charter. Often I've heard of sanctuary-men, but sanctuary children — never till now.
CARDINAL. My lord, you shall overrule my mind for once. Come on, Lord Hastings, will you go with me?
HASTINGS. I'll go, my lord.
PRINCE. Good lords, make all the speedy haste you can.
[Exeunt CARDINAL and HASTINGS.]
Say, uncle Gloucester, if our brother comes, where shall we stay until our coronation?

RICHARD. Where it seems best to your royal self. If I may advise you, for a day or two Your Highness shall rest at the Tower. Then wherever you please, and shall be thought best for your best health and recreation.
PRINCE. I don't like the Tower, of any place. Did Julius Caesar build that place, my lord?
BUCKINGHAM. He did begin that place, my gracious lord — which, since, succeeding ages have rebuilt.
PRINCE. Is it on record, or else reported successively from age to age, that he built it?
BUCKINGHAM. On record, my gracious lord.
PRINCE. But say, my lord, it weren't recorded — I think the truth should live from age to age, passed on to all posterity, even to the final all-ending day.
RICHARD.
[Aside.] So wise so young, they say, never live long.
PRINCE. What do you say, uncle?
RICHARD. I say, without written records, fame lives long.
[Aside.] Thus, like the traditional Vice, Iniquity,
I moralize two meanings into one word.

PRINCE. That Julius Caesar was a famous man. With what his valor enriched his wit, his wit set down to make his valor live. Death makes no conquest of this conqueror, for now he lives in fame, though not in life. I'll tell you what, my cousin Buckingham.
BUCKINGHAM. What, my gracious lord?
PRINCE. If I live until I'm a man, I'll win our ancient right in France again, or die a soldier, as I lived a king.
RICHARD.
[Aside.] Short summers usually have a forward spring.
[Enter young DUKE OF YORK, HASTINGS, and the CARDINAL.]
BUCKINGHAM. Now, in good time here comes the Duke of York.
PRINCE. Richard of York, how is our loving brother?
YORK. Well, my dread lord — for so I must call you now.
PRINCE. Yes, brother — to our grief, as it is to yours. He died too late, who might have kept that title, which by his death has lost much majesty.
RICHARD. How fares our cousin, noble lord of York?
YORK. I thank you, gentle uncle. Oh, my lord, you said that idle weeds grow fast. The Prince my brother has outgrown me by far.
RICHARD. He has, my lord.
YORK. And therefore is he idle?
RICHARD. Oh, my fair cousin, I mustn't say so.
YORK. Then he is more beholden to you than I am.
RICHARD. He may command me as my sovereign, but you have power over me as a kinsman.
YORK. Please, uncle, give me this dagger.
RICHARD. My dagger, little cousin? With all my heart.
PRINCE. A beggar, brother?
YORK. Of my kind uncle, who I know will give. And being just a trinket, it's no grief to give.
RICHARD. A greater gift than that I'll give my cousin.
YORK. A greater gift? Oh, that's the sword to go with it.
RICHARD. Yes, gentle cousin — if it were light enough.
YORK. Oh, then I see you'll only part with light gifts. With weightier things, you'll say no to a beggar.
RICHARD. It is too heavy for Your Grace to wear.
YORK. I'd find it light, even if it were heavier.
RICHARD. What — would you have my weapon, little lord?
YORK. I would, so that I might thank you as you call me.
RICHARD. How?
YORK. Little.
PRINCE. My lord of York is always being contrary in talk. Uncle, Your Grace knows how to bear with him.
YORK. You mean, to bear me — not bear with me. Uncle, my brother mocks both you and me. Because I'm little, like an ape, he thinks you should carry me on your shoulders.
BUCKINGHAM. With what a sharp-equipped wit he reasons! To soften the scorn he gives his uncle, he prettily and aptly taunts himself. So cunning and so young is remarkable.
RICHARD. My lord, will you please move on? Myself and my good cousin Buckingham will go to your mother, to plead with her to meet you at the Tower and welcome you.
YORK. What — will you go to the Tower, my lord?
PRINCE. My Lord Protector insists on it.
YORK. I shall not sleep in peace at the Tower.
RICHARD. Why, what should you fear?
YORK. Truly, my uncle Clarence's angry ghost. My grandmother told me he was murdered there.
PRINCE. I fear no uncles dead.
RICHARD. Nor any that live, I hope.
PRINCE. If they live, I hope I needn't fear. But come, my lord. With a heavy heart, thinking on them, I go to the Tower.
[A sennet. Exeunt PRINCE EDWARD, YORK, HASTINGS, DORSET, and all but RICHARD, BUCKINGHAM, and CATESBY.]
BUCKINGHAM. Do you think, my lord, this little prattling York wasn't incensed by his subtle mother to taunt and scorn you so opprobriously?
RICHARD. No doubt, no doubt. Oh, he's a dangerous boy — bold, quick, ingenious, forward, capable. He's all his mother's, from top to toe.

BUCKINGHAM. Well, let them rest. Come here, Catesby. You're sworn as deeply to carry out what we intend, as to closely conceal what we share. You know the reasons we discussed on the way. What do you think? Isn't it an easy matter to bring William Lord Hastings around to our way of thinking, for the installation of this noble Duke in the royal seat of this famous isle?
CATESBY. He loves the Prince so for his father's sake that he won't be won to anything against him.
BUCKINGHAM. What do you think then of Stanley? Will he?
CATESBY. He'll do everything as Hastings does.

BUCKINGHAM. Well then, no more but this: go, gentle Catesby, and, as if casually, sound out Lord Hastings to see how he's disposed to our purpose. Summon him tomorrow to the Tower to deliberate on the coronation. If you find him pliable to us, encourage him, and tell him all our reasons. If he's leaden, icy, cold, unwilling, be so too, and so break off the talk, and give us notice of his inclination. For tomorrow we hold divided councils, in which you yourself shall be highly employed.

RICHARD. Give my regards to Lord William. Tell him, Catesby, that his old knot of dangerous adversaries are tomorrow let blood at Pomfret Castle. And tell my lord, for joy of this good news, to give Mrs. Shore one gentle kiss the more.
BUCKINGHAM. Good Catesby, go and carry out this business soundly.
CATESBY. Both my good lords, with all the care I can.
RICHARD. Shall we hear from you, Catesby, before we sleep?
CATESBY. You shall, my lord.
RICHARD. At Crosby Place, you'll find us both.
[Exit CATESBY.]
