BUCKINGHAM. Now, my lord — what shall we do if we see Lord Hastings won't yield to our schemes?
RICHARD. Chop off his head, man — we'll do something. And look — when I'm king, claim from me the earldom of Hereford, and all the movables that the King my brother possessed.
BUCKINGHAM. I'll claim that promise at Your Grace's hand.
RICHARD. And expect to have it granted with all kindness. Come, let's sup early, so that afterward we may digest our schemes into some form.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 2 — Before Lord Hastings’ house
paragraphs: [Enter a MESSENGER at the door of HASTINGS.]
MESSENGER. My lord, my lord!
[Knocking.]
HASTINGS.
[Within.] Who knocks?
MESSENGER. One from Lord Stanley.
HASTINGS.
[Within.] What's the time?
MESSENGER. Just on the stroke of four.
[Enter HASTINGS.]
HASTINGS. Can't my Lord Stanley sleep these tedious nights?
MESSENGER. So it appears by what I have to say. First, he sends his regards to your noble self.
HASTINGS. And then?

MESSENGER. Then he reports to your lordship that this night he dreamt the boar had razed off his helm. Besides, he says there are two councils being held, and that something may be determined at the one that could make you and him regret things at the other. So he sends to know your lordship's pleasure — whether you will at once take horse with him and post with all speed northward, to avoid the danger his soul foresees.

HASTINGS. Go, fellow, go. Return to your lord; tell him not to fear the separate council. His honor and I are at the one, and at the other is my good friend Catesby — where nothing can proceed touching us that I will not have word of. Tell him his fears are shallow, without grounds. And as for his dreams, I'm amazed he's so simple as to trust the mockery of restless slumbers. To flee the boar before the boar pursues would be to incite the boar to follow us, and make pursuit where he meant no chase. Go, tell your master to rise and come to me, and we'll both go together to the Tower, where he'll see the boar will treat us kindly.
MESSENGER. I'll go, my lord, and tell him what you say.
[Exit.]
[Enter CATESBY.]
CATESBY. Many good mornings to my noble lord.
HASTINGS. Good morning, Catesby — you're stirring early. What news, what news in this our tottering state?
CATESBY. It is a reeling world indeed, my lord, and I believe it will never stand upright until Richard wears the garland of the realm.
HASTINGS. What — wear the garland? Do you mean the crown?
CATESBY. Yes, my good lord.
HASTINGS. I'll have this crown of mine cut from my shoulders before I'll see the crown so foully misplaced. But can you tell that he's aiming at it?

CATESBY. Yes, on my life — and he hopes to find you forward on his side for the gain of it. And thereupon he sends you this good news: that this very day your enemies, the kindred of the Queen, must die at Pomfret.

HASTINGS. Indeed, I'm no mourner for that news, since they've always been my adversaries. But that I'll give my voice on Richard's side to bar my master's heirs in true descent — God knows I will not do it, to the death.
CATESBY. God keep your lordship in that gracious mind.

HASTINGS. But I shall laugh at this a year from now — that those who brought me into my master's hate, I'll live to look upon their tragedy. Well, Catesby, before a fortnight makes me older, I'll send some packing who don't yet think of it.
CATESBY. It's a vile thing to die, my gracious lord, when men are unprepared and don't expect it.

HASTINGS. Oh, monstrous, monstrous! And so it falls out with Rivers, Vaughan, Grey — and so it will with some others who think themselves as safe as you and I, who, as you know, are dear to princely Richard and to Buckingham.
CATESBY. The Princes both make high account of you —
[Aside.] For they account his head upon the Bridge.
HASTINGS. I know they do, and I've well deserved it.
[Enter STANLEY, Earl of Derby.]
Come on, come on. Where's your boar-spear, man? Do you fear the boar, and go so unprepared?
STANLEY. My lord, good morning; good morning, Catesby. You may jest on, but, by the Holy Rood, I don't like these several councils, I don't.

HASTINGS. My lord, I hold my life as dear as you do yours, and never in my days, I assure you, was it so precious to me as it is now. Do you think, if I didn't know our state was secure, that I would be so triumphant as I am?

STANLEY. The lords at Pomfret, when they rode from London, were jovial and supposed their states were sure — and they indeed had no cause to mistrust. But yet you see how soon the day overcast. This sudden stab of rancor I distrust. I pray God, I say, that I prove a needless coward. What, shall we toward the Tower? The day is moving on.
HASTINGS. Come, come. I'll go with you. Do you know what, my lord? Today the lords you talked of are beheaded.
STANLEY. They, for their honesty, might better wear their heads than some who have accused them wear their hats. But come, my lord, let's be off.
[Enter a PURSUIVANT.]
HASTINGS. Go on ahead; I'll talk with this good fellow.
[Exeunt STANLEY and CATESBY.]
How now, sirrah? How goes the world with you?
PURSUIVANT. The better that your lordship pleases to ask.

HASTINGS. I tell you, man, it goes better with me now than when you met me last where we meet now. Then I was going as prisoner to the Tower, on the prompting of the Queen's allies. But now, I tell you — keep it to yourself — this day those enemies are put to death, and I'm in a better state than I ever was.
PURSUIVANT. May God keep it so, to your honor's good content!
HASTINGS. Many thanks, fellow. There — drink that for me.
[Throws him his purse.]
PURSUIVANT. I thank your honor.
[Exit.]
[Enter a PRIEST.]
PRIEST. Well met, my lord; I'm glad to see your honor.
HASTINGS. I thank you, good Sir John, with all my heart. I'm in your debt for your last service. Come the next Sabbath, and I'll repay you.
[Enter BUCKINGHAM.]
PRIEST. I'll attend on your lordship.
[Exit PRIEST.]
BUCKINGHAM. What — talking with a priest, Lord Chamberlain? Your friends at Pomfret, they need the priest; your honor has no shriving work on hand.
HASTINGS. Good faith, and when I met this holy man, the men you speak of came into my mind. What — are you going toward the Tower?
BUCKINGHAM. I am, my lord, but I can't stay there long. I'll return there before your lordship.
HASTINGS. No, likely enough — for I stay for dinner there.
BUCKINGHAM.
[Aside.] And supper too, although you don't know it.
Come, will you go?
HASTINGS. I'll attend on your lordship.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 3 — Pomfret. Before the Castle
paragraphs: [Enter Sir RICHARD RATCLIFFE, with halberdiers, leading the nobles RIVERS, GREY, and VAUGHAN to death at Pomfret.]
RIVERS. Sir Richard Ratcliffe, let me tell you this: today you shall see a subject die for truth, for duty, and for loyalty.
GREY. God bless the Prince from all the pack of you! You are a knot of damned bloodsuckers.
VAUGHAN. You live who shall cry woe for this hereafter.
RATCLIFFE. Dispatch. The term of your lives is up.

RIVERS. O Pomfret, Pomfret! O you bloody prison, fatal and ominous to noble peers! Within the guilty enclosure of your walls Richard the Second was hacked to death here. And, for more slander to your dismal seat, we give you our guiltless blood to drink.
GREY. Now Margaret's curse has fallen upon our heads, when she cried out on Hastings, you, and I, for standing by when Richard stabbed her son.

RIVERS. Then she cursed Richard, then she cursed Buckingham, then she cursed Hastings. Oh, remember, God, to hear her prayer for them, as now for us! And for my sister and her princely sons, be satisfied, dear God, with our true blood, which, as you know, must be unjustly spilt.
RATCLIFFE. Make haste. The hour of death has come.
RIVERS. Come, Grey, come, Vaughan, let us embrace here. Farewell, until we meet again in heaven.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 4 — London. A Room in the Tower
paragraphs: [Enter BUCKINGHAM, STANLEY Earl of Derby, HASTINGS, the BISHOP OF ELY, NORFOLK, RATCLIFFE, LOVELL, and others, at a table.]
HASTINGS. Now, noble peers, the reason we have met is to determine about the coronation. In God's name, speak — when is the royal day?
BUCKINGHAM. Is everything ready for that royal time?
STANLEY. It is, and wants only the nomination.
ELY. Tomorrow, then, I judge a happy day.
BUCKINGHAM. Who knows the Lord Protector's mind on this? Who is most intimate with the noble Duke?
ELY. Your Grace, we think, should soonest know his mind.
BUCKINGHAM. We know each other's faces; for our hearts, he knows no more of mine than I of yours, or I of his, my lord, than you of mine. Lord Hastings, you and he are close in love.

HASTINGS. I thank his Grace — I know he loves me well. But as for his purpose in the coronation, I have not sounded him, nor has he delivered his gracious pleasure in any way on it. But you, my honorable lords, may name the time, and on the Duke's behalf I'll give my voice, which I presume he'll take in gentle part.
[Enter RICHARD.]
ELY. In happy time, here comes the Duke himself.
RICHARD. My noble lords and cousins all, good morning. I have been a long sleeper; but I trust my absence has neglected no great design that by my presence might have been concluded.
BUCKINGHAM. Had you not come upon your cue, my lord, William Lord Hastings would have pronounced your part — I mean your voice for the crowning of the King.

RICHARD. No man could be bolder than my Lord Hastings. His lordship knows me well and loves me well. My lord of Ely, when I was last in Holborn I saw good strawberries in your garden there; I beg you, send for some of them.
ELY. Truly, and I will, my lord, with all my heart.
[Exit.]
RICHARD. Cousin of Buckingham, a word with you.
[They move aside.]

Catesby has sounded out Hastings on our business, and finds the testy gentleman so hot that he will lose his head before he gives consent that his master's child, as he reverently terms it, should lose the royalty of England's throne.
BUCKINGHAM. Withdraw yourself awhile. I'll go with you.
[Exeunt RICHARD and BUCKINGHAM.]
STANLEY. We have not yet set down this day of triumph. Tomorrow, in my judgment, is too sudden, for I myself am not so well prepared as I would be, were the day put off.
[Enter the BISHOP OF ELY.]
ELY. Where is my lord the Duke of Gloucester? I have sent for these strawberries.

HASTINGS. His Grace looks cheerful and smooth this morning. There's some idea or other that pleases him well, when he bids good morning with such spirit. I think there's not a man in Christendom who can less hide his love or hate than he can — for by his face you can straight tell his heart.
STANLEY. What of his heart did you perceive in his face by any indication he showed today?
HASTINGS. Truly, that with no man here is he offended — for if he were, he would have shown it in his looks.
[Enter RICHARD and BUCKINGHAM.]
RICHARD. I beg you all, tell me what they deserve who conspire my death with devilish plots of damned witchcraft, and have prevailed upon my body with their hellish charms?
HASTINGS. The tender love I bear Your Grace, my lord, makes me most forward in this princely presence to doom the offenders, whoever they be. I say, my lord, they have deserved death.

RICHARD. Then let your eyes be witness to their evil. Look how I am bewitched! Behold, my arm is like a blasted sapling, withered up! And this is Edward's wife, that monstrous witch, conspiring with that harlot, the strumpet Shore — who by their witchcraft have thus marked me.
HASTINGS. If they have done this deed, my noble lord —

RICHARD. If? You protector of this damned strumpet, you talk to me of "ifs"? You are a traitor. Off with his head! Now by Saint Paul I swear I will not dine until I see it done. Lovell and Ratcliffe, see that it's done. The rest who love me, rise and follow me.
[Exeunt all but LOVELL and RATCLIFFE with LORD HASTINGS.]

HASTINGS. Woe, woe, for England! Not a bit for me, for I, too foolish, might have prevented this. Stanley dreamt the boar did raze his helm, and I scorned it and disdained to fly. Three times today my foot-cloth horse stumbled, and started when he looked upon the Tower, as if loath to bear me to the slaughter-house. Oh, now I need the priest who spoke to me. I now repent that I told the pursuivant, too triumphantly, how my enemies today at Pomfret were bloodily butchered, and I myself secure in grace and favor. O Margaret, Margaret — now your heavy curse has lighted on poor Hastings's wretched head.
RATCLIFFE. Come, come, dispatch. The Duke would be at dinner. Make a short confession. He longs to see your head.

HASTINGS. Oh, momentary grace of mortal men, which we hunt more for than the grace of God! Whoever builds his hope on the air of your good looks lives like a drunken sailor on a mast, ready with every nod to tumble down into the fatal bowels of the deep.
LOVELL. Come, come, dispatch. It's useless to exclaim.

HASTINGS. O bloody Richard! Miserable England, I prophesy the most fearful time for you that ever wretched age has looked upon. Come, lead me to the block. Bear him my head. They smile at me who shortly shall be dead.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 5 — London. The Tower Walls
paragraphs: [Enter RICHARD and BUCKINGHAM in rotten armor, marvellously ill-favored.]
RICHARD. Come, cousin, can you quake and change your color, murder your breath in the middle of a word, and then begin again, and stop again, as if you were distraught and mad with terror?

BUCKINGHAM. Tut, I can counterfeit the deep tragedian. Speak, and look back, and peer on every side, tremble and start at the wagging of a straw, indicating deep suspicion. Ghastly looks are at my service, like forced smiles, and both are ready in their offices, at any time to grace my stratagems. But what — is Catesby gone?
RICHARD. He is. And, see, he brings the Mayor along.
[Enter the LORD MAYOR and CATESBY.]
BUCKINGHAM. Lord Mayor —
RICHARD. Look to the drawbridge there!
BUCKINGHAM. Hark, a drum.
RICHARD. Catesby, watch the walls.
BUCKINGHAM. Lord Mayor, the reason we have sent —
RICHARD. Look back! Defend yourself, here are enemies.
BUCKINGHAM. God and our innocence defend and guard us!
[Enter LOVELL and RATCLIFFE with HASTINGS's head.]
RICHARD. Be patient — they are friends, Ratcliffe and Lovell.
LOVELL. Here is the head of that ignoble traitor, the dangerous and unsuspected Hastings.

RICHARD. So dear I loved the man that I must weep. I took him for the plainest, most harmless creature that breathed upon the earth a Christian; made him my book, wherein my soul recorded the history of all her secret thoughts. So smooth he daubed his vice with show of virtue that — his apparent, open guilt omitted, I mean his affair with Shore's wife — he lived free from all taint of suspicion.

BUCKINGHAM. Well, well, he was the most covertly sheltered traitor who ever lived. Would you imagine, or almost believe — were it not that by great preservation we live to tell it — that the subtle traitor today had plotted, in the council-house, to murder me and my good lord of Gloucester?
MAYOR. Had he done so?

RICHARD. What, do you think we are Turks or infidels? Or that we would, against the form of law, proceed so rashly in the villain's death, but that the extreme peril of the case, the peace of England, and our persons' safety, forced us to this execution?
MAYOR. Now, fair befall you! He deserved his death, and your good Graces both have proceeded well, to warn false traitors from like attempts.

BUCKINGHAM. I never expected better at his hands after he once fell in with Mrs. Shore. Yet we had not determined he should die until your lordship came to see his end — which now the loving haste of these our friends, somewhat against our intentions, has prevented. Because, my lord, we would have had you hear the traitor speak, and timorously confess the manner and the purpose of his treasons, so that you might well have explained the same to the citizens, who might perhaps misconstrue us in this and wail his death.

MAYOR. But, my good lord, Your Grace's word shall serve as well as if I had seen and heard him speak. And don't doubt, right noble princes both — I'll acquaint our dutiful citizens with all your just proceedings in this case.
RICHARD. And to that end we wished your lordship here, to avoid the censures of the carping world.
BUCKINGHAM. But since you come too late for our intent, yet witness what you hear we did intend. And so, my good Lord Mayor, we bid farewell.
[Exit LORD MAYOR.]

RICHARD. Go after him, after him, cousin Buckingham. The Mayor hurries to Guildhall in all haste. There, at your most opportune moment, infer the bastardy of Edward's children. Tell them how Edward put a citizen to death only for saying he would make his son heir to the Crown — meaning indeed his house, which by its sign was so called. Moreover, press his hateful lechery and bestial appetite in change of lust, which stretched to their servants, daughters, wives, even wherever his raging eye or savage heart, without control, lusted to make a prey. Indeed, if need be, come this far near my person: tell them that when my mother was pregnant with that insatiate Edward, noble York my princely father then had wars in France, and, by true computation of the time, found that the offspring was not his begetting — which well appeared in his lineaments, being nothing like the noble Duke, my father. Yet touch this sparingly, as if from a distance — because, my lord, you know my mother lives.
BUCKINGHAM. Doubt not, my lord — I'll play the orator as if the golden fee for which I plead were for myself. And so, my lord, adieu.
RICHARD. If you thrive well, bring them to Baynard's Castle, where you'll find me well accompanied with reverend fathers and well-learned bishops.
BUCKINGHAM. I go; and toward three or four o'clock look for the news that the Guildhall affords.
[Exit.]
RICHARD. Go, Lovell, with all speed to Doctor Shaa.
[To RATCLIFFE.] Go you to Friar Penker; tell them both
to meet me within this hour at Baynard's Castle.
[Exeunt RATCLIFFE and LOVELL.]
Now I'll go take some private order to draw the brats of Clarence out of sight, and to give order that no manner of person have at any time access to the Princes.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 6 — London. A street
paragraphs: [Enter a SCRIVENER.]

SCRIVENER. Here is the indictment of the good Lord Hastings, which in a formal hand is fairly engrossed, so that it may be read out today in Paul's. And notice how neatly the sequence hangs together: I've spent eleven hours writing it out, for yesternight Catesby sent it to me. The original took just as long to do — and yet within these last five hours Hastings lived, untainted, unexamined, free, at liberty. What a fine world we live in! Who is so gross that he can't see this palpable device? Yet who is so bold as to say he sees it? The world is bad, and all will come to nothing when such ill dealing must be seen only in thought.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 7 — London. Court of Baynard’s Castle
paragraphs: [Enter RICHARD and BUCKINGHAM at separate doors.]
RICHARD. How now, how now? What do the citizens say?
BUCKINGHAM. Now, by the holy mother of our Lord, the citizens are silent — they say not a word.
RICHARD. Did you touch on the bastardy of Edward's children?

BUCKINGHAM. I did. With his contract with Lady Lucy, and his contract by proxy in France; the insatiate greediness of his desire, and his coercion of the city wives; his tyranny for trifles; his own bastardy, as having been begotten while your father was in France, and his resemblance, being unlike the Duke. Beyond this, I drew attention to your features — being the exact image of your father, both in your form and in nobleness of mind; laid open all your victories in Scotland, your discipline in war, your wisdom in peace, your bounty, virtue, fair humility. Indeed, I left nothing relevant to your purpose untouched or only slightly handled in discourse. And when my oratory drew toward its end, I bade those who loved their country's good cry, "God save Richard, England's royal King!"
RICHARD. And did they do so?

BUCKINGHAM. No, so help me God, they spoke not a word — but, like dumb statues or breathing stones, stared at each other, and looked deadly pale. When I saw that, I reproached them, and asked the Mayor what meant this willful silence. His answer was, the people were not used to being spoken to except by the Recorder. Then he was urged to tell my tale again: "Thus says the Duke, thus has the Duke argued" — but nothing spoke in warrant from himself. When he had done, some followers of my own, at the lower end of the hall, hurled up their caps, and some ten voices cried, "God save King Richard!" And so I took the advantage of those few. "Thanks, gentle citizens and friends," I said. "This general applause and cheerful shout shows your wisdom and your love to Richard." And right there I broke off and came away.
RICHARD. What, tongueless blocks they were! Wouldn't they speak? Won't the Mayor then and his colleagues come?

BUCKINGHAM. The Mayor is here at hand. Pretend some fear. Don't be spoken with except by mighty entreaty. And see that you get a prayer-book in your hand, and stand between two churchmen, good my lord, for on that ground I'll make a holy descant. And don't be easily won to our requests. Play the maid's part — keep answering no, and accept it.
RICHARD. I'll go. And if you plead as well for them as I can say no to you for myself, no doubt we'll bring it to a happy issue.
BUCKINGHAM. Go, go, up to the leads — the Lord Mayor knocks.
[Exit RICHARD.]
[Enter the LORD MAYOR and CITIZENS.]
Welcome, my lord. I'm dancing attendance here. I don't think the Duke will be spoken with.
[Enter CATESBY.]
Now, Catesby, what does your lord say to my request?

CATESBY. He begs Your Grace, my noble lord, to visit him tomorrow or the next day. He is inside, with two truly reverend fathers, devoutly bent on meditation; and on no worldly matters would he be moved to draw him from his holy exercise.

BUCKINGHAM. Return, good Catesby, to the gracious Duke. Tell him myself, the Mayor, and the aldermen, in deep designs, in a matter of great moment — no less important than our general good — have come to have some conference with His Grace.
CATESBY. I'll let him know that straight away.
[Exit.]

BUCKINGHAM. Aha, my lord — this prince is no Edward! He's not lolling on a lewd love-bed, but on his knees in meditation. Not dallying with a couple of courtesans, but meditating with two deep divines. Not sleeping, to gross his idle body, but praying, to enrich his watchful soul. Happy were England if this virtuous prince would take on His Grace the sovereignty of it. But surely I fear we shan't win him to it.
MAYOR. Truly, God forbid His Grace should refuse us!
BUCKINGHAM. I fear he will. Here comes Catesby again.
[Enter CATESBY.]
Now, Catesby, what does His Grace say?
CATESBY. He wonders why you've assembled such crowds of citizens to come to him, His Grace not having been warned of it before. He fears, my lord, you mean no good to him.
BUCKINGHAM. I'm sorry my noble cousin should suspect that I mean no good to him. By heaven, we come to him in perfect love. And so once more return and tell His Grace.
[Exit CATESBY.]
When holy and devout religious men are at their beads, it's a hard thing to draw them from it — so sweet is zealous contemplation.
[Enter RICHARD aloft, between two BISHOPS. CATESBY re-enters.]
MAYOR. See where His Grace stands between two clergymen!

BUCKINGHAM. Two props of virtue for a Christian prince, to stay him from the fall of vanity. And, see, a book of prayer in his hand — true ornaments by which to know a holy man. Famous Plantagenet, most gracious Prince, lend a favorable ear to our requests, and pardon us the interruption of your devotion and right Christian zeal.

RICHARD. My lord, there's no need for such apology. I beg Your Grace to pardon me, who, earnest in the service of my God, deferred the visit of my friends. But, leaving this, what is Your Grace's pleasure?
BUCKINGHAM. Even that which, I hope, pleases God above, and all good men of this ungoverned isle.
RICHARD. I suspect I have done some offense that appears disgraceful in the city's eye, and that you come to reprehend my ignorance.
BUCKINGHAM. You have, my lord. Would it please Your Grace, on our entreaties, to amend your fault.
RICHARD. Otherwise why do I breathe in a Christian land?

BUCKINGHAM. Know then, it is your fault that you resign the supreme seat, the throne majestical, the sceptered office of your ancestors, your state of fortune, and your due of birth, the lineal glory of your royal house, to the corruption of a blemished stock; while in the mildness of your sleepy thoughts — which here we wake to our country's good — the noble isle wants her proper limbs. Her face is defaced with scars of infamy, her royal stock grafted with ignoble plants, and almost shouldered into the swallowing gulf of dark forgetfulness and deep oblivion. To recover from which, we heartily solicit Your gracious self to take on you the charge and kingly government of this your land — not as Protector, steward, substitute, or lowly factor for another's gain, but as successively, from blood to blood, your right of birth, your empire, your own. For this, accompanied by the citizens, your very worshipful and loving friends, and by their vehement instigation, in this just cause I come to move Your Grace.

RICHARD. I cannot tell if to depart in silence, or to speak bitterly in reproof of you, best fits my standing or your condition. If not to answer, you might perhaps think tongue-tied ambition, by not replying, yielded to bear the golden yoke of sovereignty, which fondly you would here impose on me. If to reprove you for this suit of yours, so seasoned with your faithful love to me, then, on the other side, I'd be rebuking my friends. Therefore, to speak, and to avoid the first, and then, in speaking, not to incur the last, definitively thus I answer you. Your love deserves my thanks; but my desert, unmeriting, shuns your high request. First, if all obstacles were cut away, and my path were even to the crown as the ripe revenue and due of birth, yet so great is my poverty of spirit, so mighty and so many my defects, that I would rather hide myself from my greatness — being a small boat unable to bear a mighty sea — than in my greatness covet to be hidden, and smothered in the vapor of my glory. But, God be thanked, there's no need of me, and much I'd need to help you, were there need. The royal tree has left us royal fruit, which, mellowed by the stealing hours of time, will well become the seat of majesty, and make, no doubt, us happy by his reign. On him I lay what you would lay on me — the right and fortune of his happy stars — which God forbid that I should wring from him.

BUCKINGHAM. My lord, this shows conscience in Your Grace; but the considerations of it are nice and trivial, when all circumstances are well considered. You say that Edward is your brother's son; so do we, but not by Edward's wife. For first he was contracted to Lady Lucy — your mother lives a witness to his vow — and afterward by proxy betrothed to Bona, sister to the King of France. These both put aside, a poor petitioner, a care-crazed mother to many sons, a beauty-waning and distressed widow, even in the afternoon of her best days, made prize and purchase of his wanton eye, seduced the height of his degree to base descent and loathed bigamy. By her, in his unlawful bed, he begot this Edward, whom our manners call the Prince. More bitterly I could expostulate, except that, out of reverence to some alive, I give a sparing limit to my tongue. Then, good my lord, take to your royal self this proffered benefit of dignity — if not to bless us and the land along with us, yet to draw forth your noble ancestry from the corruption of abusing times into a lineal true-derived course.
MAYOR. Do, good my lord. Your citizens entreat you.
BUCKINGHAM. Don't refuse, mighty lord, this proffered love.
CATESBY. Oh, make them joyful; grant their lawful suit.
RICHARD. Alas, why would you heap those cares on me? I am unfit for state and majesty. I beg you, don't take it amiss — I cannot, nor will I, yield to you.

BUCKINGHAM. If you refuse it — as in love and zeal loath to depose the child, your brother's son — as well we know your tenderness of heart and gentle, kind, effeminate remorse, which we have noted in you to your kindred, and equally indeed to all estates — yet know, whether you accept our suit or not, your brother's son shall never reign as our king. But we will plant some other on the throne, to the disgrace and downfall of your house. And in this resolution here we leave you. Come, citizens — by God's wounds, I'll entreat no more.
[Exeunt BUCKINGHAM, the MAYOR, and citizens.]
CATESBY. Call him again, sweet Prince; accept their suit. If you deny them, all the land will rue it.
RICHARD. Will you force me to a world of cares? Call them again. I am not made of stones, but penetrable to your kind entreaties, although against my conscience and my soul.
[Enter BUCKINGHAM and the rest.]

Cousin of Buckingham, and sage grave men, since you will buckle Fortune on my back, to bear her burden, whether I will or not, I must have patience to endure the load. But if black scandal or foul-faced reproach attend the consequence of your imposition, your mere coercion shall acquit me of all the impure blots and stains of it, for God knows, and you may partly see, how far I am from the desire of this.
MAYOR. God bless Your Grace! We see it, and will say it.
RICHARD. In saying so, you shall only say the truth.
BUCKINGHAM. Then I salute you with this royal title: Long live King Richard, England's worthy King!
ALL. Amen.
BUCKINGHAM. Tomorrow may it please you to be crowned?
RICHARD. Whenever you please, since you will have it so.
BUCKINGHAM. Tomorrow, then, we'll attend Your Grace; and so most joyfully we take our leave.
RICHARD.
[To the BISHOPS.] Come, let us to our holy work again.
Farewell, my cousin, farewell, gentle friends.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 1 — London. Before the Tower
paragraphs: [Enter QUEEN ELIZABETH, the DUCHESS OF YORK, and the MARQUESS OF DORSET, at one door; ANNE Duchess of Gloucester with CLARENCE's young DAUGHTER at another door.]

DUCHESS. Who meets us here? My niece Plantagenet led by the hand of her kind aunt of Gloucester? Now, for my life, she's headed to the Tower, on pure heart's love, to greet the tender Prince. Daughter, well met.
ANNE. God give your Graces both a happy and joyful time of day.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. As much to you, good sister. Where are you headed?
ANNE. No further than the Tower, and, as I guess, upon the like devotion as yourselves — to congratulate the gentle Princes there.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Kind sister, thanks. We'll go in all together.
[Enter BRAKENBURY.]
And in good time, here comes the Lieutenant. Master Lieutenant, by your leave — how is the Prince and my young son of York?
BRAKENBURY. Right well, dear madam. By your patience, I may not allow you to visit them. The King has strictly charged the opposite.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. The King? Who's that?
BRAKENBURY. I mean the Lord Protector.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. The Lord protect him from that kingly title! Has he set bounds between their love and me? I am their mother — who shall bar me from them?
DUCHESS. I am their father's mother. I will see them.
ANNE. Their aunt I am in law, in love their mother. Then bring me to where I can see them. I'll bear your blame, and take your office from you, on my peril.
BRAKENBURY. No, madam, no. I may not leave it that way. I am bound by oath, and therefore pardon me.
[Exit.]
[Enter STANLEY.]
STANLEY. Let me but meet you, ladies, one hour from now, and I'll salute Your Grace of York as mother and reverend looker-on of two fair queens.
[To ANNE.] Come, madam, you must straight to Westminster,
there to be crowned Richard's royal queen.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Ah, cut my lace asunder, so my pent-up heart may have some room to beat, or else I swoon with this dead-killing news!
ANNE. Spiteful tidings! Oh, unpleasing news!
DORSET. Be of good cheer, mother. How is Your Grace?

QUEEN ELIZABETH. O Dorset, don't speak to me — get yourself gone. Death and destruction dog at your heels. Your mother's name is ominous to children. If you would outstrip death, go, cross the seas, and live with Richmond, beyond the reach of hell. Go, hurry, hurry from this slaughter-house, or else you'll increase the number of the dead, and make me die the slave of Margaret's curse — neither mother, wife, nor England's counted Queen.

STANLEY. Full of wise care is this your counsel, madam. Take all the swift advantage of the hours. You shall have letters from me to my son on your behalf, to meet you on the way. Don't be taken tardy by unwise delay.
DUCHESS. O ill-spreading wind of misery! O my accursed womb, the bed of death! A cockatrice you have hatched into the world, whose unavoidable eye is murderous.
STANLEY. Come, madam, come. I was sent in all haste.

ANNE. And I, with all unwillingness, will go. Oh, would to God that the enclosing rim of golden metal that must round my brow were red-hot steel, to sear me to the brains. Let me be anointed with deadly venom, and die before men can say "God save the Queen."
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Go, go, poor soul; I do not envy your glory. To indulge my mood, don't wish yourself any harm.

ANNE. No? Why? When he who is my husband now came to me as I followed Henry's corpse, when scarcely the blood was washed from his hands that flowed from my other angel husband, and that dear saint whom I then weeping followed — oh, when, I say, I looked on Richard's face, this was my wish: "Be you," said I, "accursed for making me, so young, so old a widow; and when you wed, let sorrow haunt your bed; and let your wife — if any be so mad — be more miserable by the life of you than you have made me by my dear lord's death." Lo, before I could repeat this curse again, within so small a time, my woman's heart grossly grew captive to his honey words, and proved the subject of my own soul's curse — which till now has kept my eyes from rest. For never yet one hour in his bed did I enjoy the golden dew of sleep, but with his fearful dreams I was still awakened. Besides, he hates me for my father Warwick, and will, no doubt, shortly be rid of me.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Poor heart, adieu — I pity your complaining.
ANNE. No more than with my soul I mourn for yours.
DORSET. Farewell, you woeful welcomer of glory.
ANNE. Adieu, poor soul, who takes your leave of it.
DUCHESS.
[To DORSET.] Go you to Richmond, and good fortune guide you.
[To ANNE.] Go you to Richard, and good angels tend you.
[To QUEEN ELIZABETH.] Go you to sanctuary, and good thoughts possess
you. I to my grave, where peace and rest lie with me. Eighty-odd years of sorrow I have seen, and each hour's joy wrecked with a week of woe.

QUEEN ELIZABETH. Wait — yet look back with me toward the Tower. Pity, you ancient stones, those tender babes whom envy has immured within your walls. Rough cradle for such little pretty ones, rude ragged nurse, old sullen playfellow for tender princes — treat my babies well. So foolish sorrow bids your stones farewell.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 2 — London. A Room of State in the Palace
paragraphs: [The trumpets sound a sennet. Enter RICHARD in pomp, BUCKINGHAM, CATESBY, RATCLIFFE, LOVELL, a PAGE, and others.]
KING RICHARD. Stand all apart. Cousin of Buckingham!
BUCKINGHAM. My gracious sovereign!
KING RICHARD. Give me your hand.
[Here he ascends the throne. Sound trumpets.]
Thus high, by your advice and your assistance, is King Richard seated. But shall we wear these glories for a day, or shall they last, and we rejoice in them?
BUCKINGHAM. May they live still, and forever let them last!
KING RICHARD. Ah, Buckingham, now I play the touchstone, to try whether you are current gold indeed. Young Edward lives — think now what I would say.
BUCKINGHAM. Say on, my loving lord.
KING RICHARD. Why, Buckingham, I say I would be King.
BUCKINGHAM. Why, so you are, my thrice-renowned lord.
KING RICHARD. Ha! Am I King? So it is — but Edward lives.
BUCKINGHAM. True, noble Prince.

KING RICHARD. O bitter consequence — that Edward should still live "true noble prince"! Cousin, you weren't used to being so dull. Shall I be plain? I wish the bastards dead, and I would have it done suddenly. What do you say now? Speak suddenly, be brief.
BUCKINGHAM. Your Grace may do your pleasure.
KING RICHARD. Tut, tut, you are all ice; your kindness freezes. Say, do I have your consent that they shall die?
BUCKINGHAM. Give me some little breath, some pause, dear lord, before I positively speak on this. I'll resolve you on this presently.
[Exit.]
CATESBY.
[Aside.] The King is angry. See, he gnaws his lip.
KING RICHARD.
[Aside.] I will deal with iron-witted fools
and unreflecting boys. None are for me who look into me with thoughtful eyes. High-reaching Buckingham grows circumspect. Boy!
PAGE. My lord?
KING RICHARD. Don't you know any whom corrupting gold will tempt to a secret exploit of death?
PAGE. I know a discontented gentleman whose humble means don't match his haughty spirit. Gold would be as good as twenty orators, and will no doubt tempt him to anything.
KING RICHARD. What is his name?
PAGE. His name, my lord, is Tyrrel.
KING RICHARD. I partly know the man. Go, call him here, boy.
[Exit PAGE.]
[Aside.] The deep-revolving witty Buckingham
shall no more be the neighbor to my counsels. Has he held out with me so long, untired, and stops he now for breath? Well, so be it.
[Enter STANLEY.]
How now, Lord Stanley, what's the news?
STANLEY. Know, my loving lord — the Marquess Dorset, as I hear, has fled to Richmond, in the parts where he stays.

KING RICHARD. Come here, Catesby. Spread the rumor abroad that Anne my wife is very gravely sick. I will take order for her being kept close. Find me out some mean poor gentleman, whom I will marry straight to Clarence's daughter. The boy is foolish, and I fear him not. Look how you stare! I say again, put it about that Anne, my Queen, is sick and likely to die. About it — for it stands me much upon to stop all hopes whose growth might damage me.
[Exit CATESBY.]

I must be married to my brother's daughter, or else my kingdom stands on brittle glass. Murder her brothers, and then marry her — uncertain way of gain! But I am in so far in blood that sin will pluck on sin. Tear-falling pity dwells not in this eye.
[Enter TYRREL.]
Is your name Tyrrel?
TYRREL. James Tyrrel, and your most obedient subject.
KING RICHARD. Are you indeed?
TYRREL. Prove me, my gracious lord.
KING RICHARD. Dare you resolve to kill a friend of mine?
TYRREL. If you please. But I'd rather kill two enemies.
KING RICHARD. Why then you have it — two deep enemies, foes to my rest, and disturbers of my sweet sleep, are those I would have you deal with. Tyrrel, I mean those bastards in the Tower.
TYRREL. Let me have open access to come to them, and soon I'll rid you of the fear of them.
KING RICHARD. You sing sweet music. Listen — come here, Tyrrel. Go, by this token. Rise, and lend your ear.
[Whispers.] There's no more but that. Say it is done,
and I will love you, and advance you for it.
TYRREL. I'll dispatch it straight.
[Exit.]
[Enter BUCKINGHAM.]
BUCKINGHAM. My lord, I have considered in my mind the recent request you sounded me on.
KING RICHARD. Well, let that rest. Dorset has fled to Richmond.
BUCKINGHAM. I hear the news, my lord.
KING RICHARD. Stanley, he is your wife's son. Well, see to it.
BUCKINGHAM. My lord, I claim the gift, my due by promise, for which your honor and your faith are pledged: the earldom of Hereford, and the movables you have promised I should possess.
KING RICHARD. Stanley, look to your wife. If she conveys letters to Richmond, you shall answer for it.
BUCKINGHAM. What does Your Highness say to my just request?
KING RICHARD. I do recall — Henry the Sixth did prophesy that Richmond should be King, when Richmond was a little peevish boy. A king, perhaps —
BUCKINGHAM. My lord —
KING RICHARD. How is it the prophet couldn't at that time have told me, with me there, that I should kill him?
BUCKINGHAM. My lord, your promise for the earldom —

KING RICHARD. Richmond! When I was last at Exeter, the Mayor in courtesy showed me the castle and called it Rougemont — at which name I started, because a bard of Ireland told me once I should not live long after I saw Richmond.
BUCKINGHAM. My lord —
KING RICHARD. Yes, what's the time?
BUCKINGHAM. I am thus bold as to put Your Grace in mind of what you promised me.
KING RICHARD. Well, but what's the time?
BUCKINGHAM. Upon the stroke of ten.
KING RICHARD. Well, let it strike.
BUCKINGHAM. Why let it strike?
KING RICHARD. Because, like a clockwork figure, you keep the stroke between your begging and my meditation. I am not in the giving vein today.
BUCKINGHAM. Why then, resolve me whether you will or not.
KING RICHARD. You trouble me. I am not in the vein.
[Exit, followed by all but BUCKINGHAM.]
BUCKINGHAM. And is it thus? Does he repay my deep service with such contempt? Did I make him King for this? Oh, let me think on Hastings, and be gone to Brecknock while my fearful head is still on!
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 3 — London. Another Room in the Palace
paragraphs: [Enter TYRREL.]

TYRREL. The tyrannous and bloody act is done — the most arch deed of piteous massacre that ever yet this land was guilty of. Dighton and Forrest, whom I suborned to do this piece of ruthless butchery, although they were hardened villains, bloody dogs, melted with tenderness and mild compassion, wept like two children at the sad story of their deaths. "Oh, thus," said Dighton, "lay the gentle babes;" "Thus, thus," said Forrest, "girdling one another within their alabaster innocent arms. Their lips were four red roses on a stalk, and in their summer beauty kissed each other. A book of prayers on their pillow lay — which once," said Forrest, "almost changed my mind. But, oh, the devil —" There the villain stopped; when Dighton thus went on: "We smothered the most well-furnished sweet work of nature that from the first creation she ever framed." From there both have gone with conscience and remorse — they could not speak. And so I left them both to bear this tidings to the bloody King.
[Enter KING RICHARD.]
And here he comes. All health, my sovereign lord.
KING RICHARD. Kind Tyrrel, am I happy in your news?
TYRREL. If to have done the thing you gave me in charge brings your happiness, be happy then, for it is done.
KING RICHARD. But did you see them dead?
TYRREL. I did, my lord.
KING RICHARD. And buried, gentle Tyrrel?
TYRREL. The chaplain of the Tower has buried them, but where, to say the truth, I don't know.

KING RICHARD. Come to me, Tyrrel, soon, just after supper, when you shall tell me the process of their death. Meantime, just think how I may do you good, and be inheritor of your desire. Farewell till then.
TYRREL. I humbly take my leave.
[Exit.]

KING RICHARD. The son of Clarence I have pent up close; his daughter I have matched in mean marriage; the sons of Edward sleep in Abraham's bosom; and Anne my wife has bid the world good night. Now, since I know the Breton Richmond aims at young Elizabeth, my brother's daughter, and by that knot looks proudly on the crown — to her I go, a jolly thriving wooer.
[Enter RATCLIFFE.]
RATCLIFFE. My lord!
KING RICHARD. Good or bad news, that you come in so bluntly?
RATCLIFFE. Bad news, my lord. Morton has fled to Richmond, and Buckingham, backed by the hardy Welshmen, is in the field, and still his power increases.

KING RICHARD. Ely with Richmond troubles me more nearly than Buckingham and his hastily levied force. Come — I have learned that fearful commenting is leaden servant to dull delay; delay leads to impotent and snail-paced beggary. Then fiery dispatch be my wing — Jove's Mercury, and herald for a king! Go, muster men. My counsel is my shield. We must be brief when traitors brave the field.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 4 — London. Before the Palace
paragraphs: [Enter old QUEEN MARGARET.]

QUEEN MARGARET. So now prosperity begins to mellow, and drop into the rotten mouth of death. Here in these confines I have slyly lurked to watch the waning of my enemies. A dire introduction I am witness to, and I'll go to France, hoping the consequence will prove as bitter, black, and tragical. Withdraw yourself, wretched Margaret. Who comes here?
[Retires.]
[Enter DUCHESS OF YORK and QUEEN ELIZABETH.]

QUEEN ELIZABETH. Ah, my poor Princes! Ah, my tender babes, my unblown flowers, new-appearing sweetnesses! If your gentle souls yet fly in the air and aren't fixed in perpetual doom, hover about me with your airy wings and hear your mother's lamentation.
QUEEN MARGARET.
[Aside.] Hover about her; say that right for right
has dimmed your infant morn to aged night.
DUCHESS. So many miseries have crazed my voice that my woe-wearied tongue is still and mute. Edward Plantagenet, why are you dead?
QUEEN MARGARET.
[Aside.] Plantagenet repays Plantagenet;
Edward for Edward pays a dying debt.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Would you, O God, fly from such gentle lambs and throw them into the entrails of the wolf? When did you sleep when such a deed was done?
QUEEN MARGARET.
[Aside.] When holy Harry died, and my sweet son.

DUCHESS. Dead life, blind sight, poor mortal living ghost, woe's scene, world's shame, the grave's due usurped by life, brief abstract and record of tedious days, rest your unrest on England's lawful earth,
[Sitting.] unlawfully made drunk with innocent blood.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Ah, that you would as soon afford a grave as you can yield a melancholy seat — then I would hide my bones, not rest them here.
[Sitting.] Ah, who has any cause to mourn but we?
QUEEN MARGARET.
[Coming forward.]
If ancient sorrow be most reverend, give mine the benefit of seniority, and let my griefs frown on the upper hand. If sorrow can admit company,
[Sitting down with them.]

tell over your woes again by viewing mine. I had an Edward, till a Richard killed him; I had a husband, till a Richard killed him. You had an Edward, till a Richard killed him; you had a Richard, till a Richard killed him.
DUCHESS. I had a Richard too, and you did kill him. I had a Rutland too; you helped to kill him.

QUEEN MARGARET. You had a Clarence too, and Richard killed him. From the kennel of your womb has crept a hellhound that hunts us all to death — that dog, that had his teeth before his eyes, to worry lambs and lap their gentle blood; that excellent grand tyrant of the earth, that reigns in the galled eyes of weeping souls; that foul defacer of God's handiwork your womb let loose to chase us to our graves. O upright, just, and true-disposing God, how I thank you that this carnal cur preys on the issue of his mother's body, and makes her share the bench of others' mourning!
DUCHESS. O Harry's wife, don't triumph in my woes! God witness with me, I have wept for yours.

QUEEN MARGARET. Bear with me. I am hungry for revenge, and now I sate myself with beholding it. Your Edward is dead, who killed my Edward; the other Edward dead, to pay for my Edward; young York, he is but a make-weight, because the two of them together did not match the high perfection of my loss. Your Clarence is dead, who stabbed my Edward; and the beholders of this frantic play — the adulterate Hastings, Rivers, Vaughan, Grey — untimely smothered in their dusky graves. Richard yet lives, hell's black agent — only kept as their factor to buy souls and send them there. But at hand, at hand follows his piteous and unpitied end. Earth gapes, hell burns, fiends roar, saints pray, to have him suddenly taken from here. Cancel his bond of life, dear God, I pray, that I may live to say "The dog is dead."
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Oh, you did prophesy the time would come that I should wish for you to help me curse that bottled spider, that foul hunch-backed toad!

QUEEN MARGARET. I called you then a vain flourish of my fortune; I called you then poor shadow, painted queen, the presentation of only what I was, the flattering index of a dire pageant — one heaved up high to be hurled down below, a mother only mocked with two fair babes, a dream of what you were; a garish flag, to be the aim of every dangerous shot; a sign of dignity, a breath, a bubble; a queen in jest, only to fill the scene. Where is your husband now? Where are your brothers? Where are your two sons? In what do you take joy? Who sues, and kneels, and says, "God save the Queen"? Where are the bending peers that flattered you? Where are the thronging troops that followed you? Decline all this, and see what you now are: for happy wife, a most distressed widow; for joyful mother, one that wails the name; for one being sued to, one that humbly sues; for Queen, a very wretch crowned with care; for she who scorned me, now scorned by me; for she who was feared by all, now fearing one; for she commanding all, obeyed by none. Thus has the course of justice wheeled about and left you only as a very prey to time, with nothing more than the thought of what you were to torture you the more, being what you are. You usurped my place, and don't you usurp the just proportion of my sorrow? Now your proud neck bears half my burdened yoke, from which even here I slip my weary head, and leave the burden of it all on you. Farewell, York's wife, and Queen of sad mischance. These English woes shall make me smile in France.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Oh you well skilled in curses, stay a while, and teach me how to curse my enemies.

QUEEN MARGARET. Forbear to sleep the night, and fast the days; compare dead happiness with living woe; think that your babes were sweeter than they were, and he who slew them fouler than he is. Bettering your loss makes the bad-causer worse. Revolving this will teach you how to curse.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. My words are dull. Oh, quicken them with yours!
QUEEN MARGARET. Your woes will make them sharp, and pierce like mine.
[Exit.]
DUCHESS. Why should calamity be full of words?

QUEEN ELIZABETH. Windy attorneys to their clients' woes, airy successors of intestate joys, poor breathing orators of miseries — let them have scope, though what they impart helps nothing else, yet they do ease the heart.
DUCHESS. If so, then don't be tongue-tied. Come with me, and in the breath of bitter words let's smother my damned son, who smothered your two sweet sons.
[A trumpet sounds.]
The trumpet sounds. Be copious in exclamations.
[Enter KING RICHARD and his train, including CATESBY, marching.]
KING RICHARD. Who intercepts me in my expedition?
DUCHESS. Oh, she who might have intercepted you, by strangling you in her accursed womb, from all the slaughters, wretch, that you have done.

QUEEN ELIZABETH. Do you hide that forehead with a golden crown where should be branded — if right were right — the slaughter of the Prince that owned that crown, and the dire death of my poor sons and brothers? Tell me, you villain-slave, where are my children?
DUCHESS. You toad, you toad, where is your brother Clarence, and little Ned Plantagenet, his son?
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Where is the gentle Rivers, Vaughan, Grey?
DUCHESS. Where is kind Hastings?
KING RICHARD. A flourish, trumpets! Strike alarum, drums! Don't let the heavens hear these tell-tale women rail on the Lord's anointed. Strike, I say!
[Flourish. Alarums.]
Either be patient and entreat me fair, or with the clamorous report of war thus I will drown your exclamations.
DUCHESS. Are you my son?
KING RICHARD. Yes — I thank God, my father, and you.
DUCHESS. Then patiently hear my impatience.
KING RICHARD. Madam, I have a touch of your condition, that cannot bear the tone of reproof.
DUCHESS. Oh, let me speak!
KING RICHARD. Do then, but I'll not hear.
DUCHESS. I will be mild and gentle in my words.
KING RICHARD. And brief, good mother, for I am in haste.
DUCHESS. Are you so hasty? I have waited for you, God knows, in torment and in agony.
KING RICHARD. And didn't I come at last to comfort you?

DUCHESS. No, by the Holy Rood, you know it well — you came on earth to make the earth my hell. A grievous burden was your birth to me; touchy and wayward was your infancy; your school-days frightful, desperate, wild, and furious; your prime of manhood daring, bold, and venturous; your settled age proud, subtle, sly, and bloody, more mild but yet more harmful, kind in hatred. What comfortable hour can you name that ever graced me with your company?

KING RICHARD. Truly, none but Humphrey Hower, who called Your Grace to breakfast once, out of my company. If I am so disgraceful in your eye, let me march on and not offend you, madam. Strike up the drum.
DUCHESS. Please, hear me speak.
KING RICHARD. You speak too bitterly.
DUCHESS. Hear me a word — for I shall never speak to you again.
KING RICHARD. So.

DUCHESS. Either you will die by God's just ordinance before you turn from this war a conqueror, or I with grief and extreme old age shall perish, and never more behold your face again. Therefore take with you my most grievous curse, which on the day of battle shall tire you more than all the complete armor that you wear. My prayers fight on the opposing side; and there the little souls of Edward's children whisper to the spirits of your enemies and promise them success and victory. Bloody you are; bloody will be your end. Shame attends your life and waits on your death.
[Exit.]
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Though far more cause, yet much less spirit to curse remains in me, I say amen to her.
KING RICHARD. Wait, madam — I must have a word with you.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. I have no more sons of the royal blood for you to slaughter. As for my daughters, Richard, they shall be praying nuns, not weeping queens. So don't aim to take their lives.
KING RICHARD. You have a daughter called Elizabeth, virtuous and fair, royal and gracious.

QUEEN ELIZABETH. And must she die for this? Oh, let her live, and I'll corrupt her manners, stain her beauty, slander myself as false to Edward's bed, throw over her the veil of infamy. So she may live unscarred of bleeding slaughter, I will confess she was not Edward's daughter.
KING RICHARD. Don't wrong her birth — she is a royal princess.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. To save her life, I'll say she is not.
KING RICHARD. Her life is safest only in her birth.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. And only in that safety died her brothers.
KING RICHARD. Look, at their births good stars were opposite.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. No, to their lives ill friends were contrary.
KING RICHARD. All unavoided is the doom of destiny.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. True, when avoided grace makes destiny. My babes were destined to a fairer death, if grace had blessed you with a fairer life.
KING RICHARD. You speak as if I had slain my cousins.

QUEEN ELIZABETH. Cousins, indeed — and by their uncle cozened of comfort, kingdom, kindred, freedom, life. Whose hand soever lanced their tender hearts, your head, all indirectly, gave direction. No doubt the murderous knife was dull and blunt till it was whetted on your stone-hard heart, to revel in the entrails of my lambs. But that constant practice of grief makes wild grief tame, my tongue would not name my boys to your ears till my nails were anchored in your eyes, and I, in such a desperate bay of death, like a poor bark robbed of sails and tackling, dashed all to pieces on your rocky bosom.
KING RICHARD. Madam, so may I thrive in my enterprise and dangerous success of bloody wars, as I intend more good to you and yours than ever you or yours have been harmed by me!
QUEEN ELIZABETH. What good is covered by the face of heaven, waiting to be discovered, that can do me good?
KING RICHARD. The advancement of your children, gentle lady.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Up to some scaffold, there to lose their heads.
KING RICHARD. To the dignity and height of fortune, the high imperial type of this earth's glory.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Flatter my sorrows with a report of it. Tell me what state, what dignity, what honor, can you bestow on any child of mine?
KING RICHARD. Everything I have — yes, and myself and all, will I endow on a child of yours. So in the Lethe of your angry soul drown the sad memory of those wrongs which you suppose I have done you.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Be brief, lest the process of your kindness last longer in the telling than your kindness lasts.
KING RICHARD. Then know, that from my soul I love your daughter.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. My daughter's mother thinks it with her soul.
KING RICHARD. What do you think?
QUEEN ELIZABETH. That you love my daughter from your soul. From your soul's love you also loved her brothers, and from my heart's love I thank you for it.
KING RICHARD. Don't be so hasty to confound my meaning. I mean that with my soul I love your daughter, and intend to make her Queen of England.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Well then, who do you mean shall be her king?
KING RICHARD. Even he who makes her Queen. Who else should be?
QUEEN ELIZABETH. What, you?
KING RICHARD. Even so. What do you think of it?
QUEEN ELIZABETH. How can you woo her?
KING RICHARD. That I would learn from you, as the one best acquainted with her temperament.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. And will you learn from me?
KING RICHARD. Madam, with all my heart.

QUEEN ELIZABETH. Send to her, by the man who slew her brothers, a pair of bleeding hearts. On them engrave "Edward" and "York." Then perhaps she'll weep. Therefore present to her — as sometimes Margaret did to your father, steeped in Rutland's blood — a handkerchief, which, tell her, did drain the purple sap from her sweet brothers' bodies, and bid her wipe her weeping eyes with it. If this inducement doesn't move her to love, send her a letter of your noble deeds. Tell her you did away with her uncle Clarence, her uncle Rivers — yes, and for her sake made quick conveyance of her good aunt Anne.
KING RICHARD. You mock me, madam — this is not the way to win your daughter.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. There is no other way, unless you could put on some other shape, and not be Richard, who has done all this.
KING RICHARD. Say that I did all this for love of her?
QUEEN ELIZABETH. No, then indeed she cannot choose but hate you, having bought love with such a bloody spoil.

KING RICHARD. Look, what is done cannot now be amended. Men shall deal unwisely sometimes, which after-hours give leisure to repent. If I took the kingdom from your sons, to make amends I'll give it to your daughter. If I have killed the issue of your womb, to quicken your increase I will beget my issue of your blood upon your daughter. A grandmother's name is little less in love than is the doting title of a mother. They are as children but one step below, even of your mettle, of your very blood — all the same pain, save for a night of groans endured by her, for whom you suffered like sorrow. Your children were vexation to your youth, but mine shall be a comfort to your age. The loss you have is only a son being King, and by that loss your daughter is made Queen. I cannot make you what amends I would; therefore accept such kindness as I can. Dorset, your son, who with a fearful soul leads discontented steps in foreign soil, this fair alliance shall quickly call home to high promotions and great dignity. The King, who calls your beauteous daughter wife, shall familiarly call your Dorset brother. Again you shall be mother to a king, and all the ruins of distressful times repaired with double riches of content. What — we have many goodly days to see. The liquid drops of tears you have shed shall come again, transformed to oriental pearl, advantaging their loan with the interest of ten times double gain of happiness. Go then, my mother — go to your daughter. Make bold her bashful years with your experience; prepare her ears to hear a wooer's tale; put in her tender heart the aspiring flame of golden sovereignty; acquaint the Princess with the sweet silent hours of marriage joys. And when this arm of mine has chastised the petty rebel, dull-brained Buckingham, bound with triumphant garlands I will come and lead your daughter to a conqueror's bed; to whom I will retail my conquest won, and she shall be sole victoress, Caesar's Caesar.

QUEEN ELIZABETH. What would I best say? That her father's brother would be her lord? Or shall I say her uncle? Or he who slew her brothers and her uncles? Under what title shall I woo for you, that God, the law, my honor, and her love can make seem pleasing to her tender years?
KING RICHARD. Argue fair England's peace by this alliance.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Which she shall purchase with still-lasting war.
KING RICHARD. Tell her the King, who could command, entreats.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. That at her hands which the King's King forbids.
KING RICHARD. Say she shall be a high and mighty queen.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. To debase the title, as her mother does.
KING RICHARD. Say I will love her everlastingly.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. But how long shall that title "ever" last?
KING RICHARD. Sweetly in force to her fair life's end.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. But how long fairly shall her sweet life last?
KING RICHARD. As long as heaven and nature lengthens it.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. As long as hell and Richard likes of it.
KING RICHARD. Say I, her sovereign, am her humble subject.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. But she, your subject, loathes such sovereignty.
KING RICHARD. Be eloquent on my behalf to her.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. An honest tale speeds best being plainly told.
KING RICHARD. Then plainly tell her my loving tale.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Plain and not honest is too harsh a style.
KING RICHARD. Your reasons are too shallow and too quick.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Oh no — my reasons are too deep and dead. Too deep and dead, poor infants, in their graves.
KING RICHARD. Don't harp on that string, madam — that is past.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Harp on it I shall till heart-strings break.
KING RICHARD. Now, by my George, my Garter, and my crown —
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Profaned, dishonored, and the third usurped.
KING RICHARD. I swear —

QUEEN ELIZABETH. By nothing, for this is no oath. Your George, profaned, has lost his lordly honor; your Garter, blemished, has pawned its knightly virtue; your crown, usurped, has disgraced its kingly glory. If you would swear by something to be believed, swear then by something you have not wronged.
KING RICHARD. Now, by the world —
QUEEN ELIZABETH. It is full of your foul wrongs.
KING RICHARD. My father's death —
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Your life has dishonored that.
KING RICHARD. Then, by myself —
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Yourself is self-misused.
KING RICHARD. Why, then, by God —

QUEEN ELIZABETH. God's wrong is most of all. If you had feared to break an oath with him, the unity the King my husband made you would not have broken, nor would my brothers have died. If you had feared to break an oath by him, the imperial metal now circling your head would have graced the tender temples of my child, and both the Princes would have been breathing here — who now, two tender bedfellows for dust, your broken faith has made a prey for worms. What can you swear by now?
KING RICHARD. The time to come.

QUEEN ELIZABETH. That you have wronged in the time past, for I myself have many tears to wash the future, for time past wronged by you. The children live whose fathers you have slaughtered, ungoverned youth, to wail it in their age. The parents live whose children you have butchered, old barren plants, to wail it with their age. Don't swear by time to come, for that you have misused before it could be used, by times ill-used and past.

KING RICHARD. As I intend to prosper and repent, so may I thrive in my dangerous affairs of hostile arms! Myself, may I confound myself! May heaven and fortune bar me from happy hours! Day, yield me not your light, nor, night, your rest! Let all planets of good luck be opposite to my proceedings, if with dear heart's love, immaculate devotion, holy thoughts, I do not court your beauteous princely daughter. In her consists my happiness and yours. Without her follows to myself and you, herself, the land, and many a Christian soul — death, desolation, ruin, and decay. It cannot be avoided but by this; it will not be avoided but by this. Therefore, dear mother — I must call you so — be the attorney of my love to her. Plead what I will be, not what I have been; not my deserts, but what I will deserve. Press the necessity and state of times, and don't be found peevish in great designs.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Shall I be tempted by the devil thus?
KING RICHARD. Yes, if the devil tempts you to do good.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Shall I forget myself to be myself?
KING RICHARD. Yes, if your self's remembrance wrongs yourself.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Yet you killed my children.
KING RICHARD. But in your daughter's womb I bury them, where, in that nest of spicery, they will breed selves of themselves, to your recomfort.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Shall I go and win my daughter to your will?
KING RICHARD. And be a happy mother by the deed.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. I go. Write to me very shortly, and from me you shall understand her mind.
KING RICHARD. Bear her my true love's kiss; and so, farewell.
[Kissing her. Exit QUEEN ELIZABETH.]
Relenting fool, and shallow, changing woman!
[Enter RATCLIFFE.]
How now, what news?

RATCLIFFE. Most mighty sovereign, on the western coast a puissant navy is sailing. To our shores throng many doubtful, hollow-hearted friends, unarmed, and unresolved to beat them back. It's thought that Richmond is their admiral; and there they wait at anchor, expecting only the aid of Buckingham to welcome them ashore.
KING RICHARD. Some light-foot friend post to the Duke of Norfolk. Ratcliffe, yourself, or Catesby. Where is he?
CATESBY. Here, my good lord.
KING RICHARD. Catesby, fly to the Duke.
CATESBY. I will, my lord, with all convenient haste.
KING RICHARD. Ratcliffe, come here. Post to Salisbury. When you come there —
[To CATESBY.] Dull, unmindful villain,
why do you stay here, and don't go to the Duke?
CATESBY. First, mighty liege, tell me Your Highness's pleasure — what from Your Grace shall I deliver to him.
KING RICHARD. Oh, true, good Catesby. Tell him to levy at once the greatest strength and power he can make, and meet me suddenly at Salisbury.
CATESBY. I go.
[Exit.]
RATCLIFFE. What, may it please you, shall I do at Salisbury?
KING RICHARD. Why, what would you do there before I go?
RATCLIFFE. Your Highness told me I should post on ahead.
KING RICHARD. My mind has changed.
[Enter STANLEY, Earl of Derby.]
Stanley, what news from you?
STANLEY. None good, my liege, to please you with the hearing; nor any so bad but may well be reported.
KING RICHARD. Heyday, a riddle! Neither good nor bad. What need you go so many miles around when you might tell your tale the nearest way? Once more — what news?
STANLEY. Richmond is on the seas.
KING RICHARD. There let him sink, and be the seas on him! White-livered runaway, what does he do there?
STANLEY. I don't know, mighty sovereign, except by guess.
KING RICHARD. Well — as you guess?
STANLEY. Stirred up by Dorset, Buckingham, and Morton, he makes for England, here to claim the crown.

KING RICHARD. Is the chair empty? Is the sword unswayed? Is the King dead? The empire unpossessed? What heir of York is there alive but we? And who is England's King but great York's heir? Then tell me — what makes him on the seas?
STANLEY. Unless for that, my liege, I cannot guess.
KING RICHARD. Unless he comes to be your liege, you cannot guess why the Welshman comes. You will revolt and fly to him, I fear.
STANLEY. No, my good lord. So don't mistrust me.
KING RICHARD. Where is your power, then, to beat him back? Where are your tenants and your followers? Aren't they now on the western shore, safe-conducting the rebels from their ships?
STANLEY. No, my good lord — my friends are in the north.
KING RICHARD. Cold friends to me. What do they do in the north, when they should serve their sovereign in the west?
STANLEY. They have not been commanded, mighty King. If it pleases Your Majesty to give me leave, I'll muster up my friends, and meet Your Grace where and at what time Your Majesty shall please.
KING RICHARD. Yes, yes — you would be gone to join with Richmond. But I won't trust you.
STANLEY. Most mighty sovereign, you have no cause to hold my friendship doubtful. I never was, nor ever will be, false.
KING RICHARD. Go then, and muster men, but leave behind your son George Stanley. See that your heart is firm, or else his head's assurance is but frail.
STANLEY. Deal with him as I prove true to you.
[Exit.]
[Enter a MESSENGER.]

MESSENGER. My gracious sovereign, now in Devonshire, as I am well advised by friends, Sir Edward Courtney and the haughty prelate, the Bishop of Exeter, his elder brother, with many more confederates, are in arms.
[Enter another MESSENGER.]
SECOND MESSENGER. In Kent, my liege, the Guilfords are in arms, and every hour more rivals flock to the rebels, and their power grows strong.
[Enter another MESSENGER.]
THIRD MESSENGER. My lord, the army of great Buckingham —
KING RICHARD. Out on you, owls! Nothing but songs of death?
[He strikes him.]
There, take that till you bring better news.

THIRD MESSENGER. The news I have to tell Your Majesty is, that by sudden floods and falling of waters, Buckingham's army is dispersed and scattered, and he himself has wandered away alone, no man knows where.
KING RICHARD. I beg your pardon. There is my purse to cure that blow of yours. Has any well-advised friend proclaimed a reward to him that brings the traitor in?
THIRD MESSENGER. Such proclamation has been made, my lord.
[Enter another MESSENGER.]

FOURTH MESSENGER. Sir Thomas Lovell and Lord Marquess Dorset, it is said, my liege, are in arms in Yorkshire. But this good comfort I bring to Your Highness: the Breton navy is dispersed by tempest. Richmond, in Dorsetshire, sent out a boat to the shore, to ask those on the banks whether they were his supporters, yes or no? Who answered him they came from Buckingham, on his side. He, mistrusting them, hoisted sail, and made his course again for Brittany.
KING RICHARD. March on, march on, since we are up in arms — if not to fight with foreign enemies, yet to beat down these rebels here at home.
[Enter CATESBY.]
CATESBY. My liege, the Duke of Buckingham is taken. That is the best news. That the Earl of Richmond has landed with a mighty force at Milford is colder tidings, yet they must be told.
KING RICHARD. Away towards Salisbury! While we reason here a royal battle might be won and lost. Someone take order that Buckingham be brought to Salisbury; the rest march on with me.
[Flourish. Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 5 — A Room in Lord Stanley’s house
paragraphs: [Enter STANLEY, Earl of Derby, and Sir CHRISTOPHER URSWICK.]

STANLEY. Sir Christopher, tell Richmond this from me: that in the sty of the most deadly boar my son George Stanley is pent up in hold. If I revolt, off goes young George's head. The fear of that holds off my present aid. So go your way. Give my regards to your lord. Also say that the Queen has heartily consented that he should marry Elizabeth, her daughter. But tell me — where is princely Richmond now?
CHRISTOPHER. At Pembroke, or at Haverfordwest in Wales.
STANLEY. What men of name resort to him?

CHRISTOPHER. Sir Walter Herbert, a renowned soldier; Sir Gilbert Talbot, Sir William Stanley, Oxford, redoubted Pembroke, Sir James Blunt, and Rice ap Thomas, with a valiant crew, and many others of great name and worth. And they bend their power toward London, if they aren't fought on the way.
STANLEY. Well, hurry to your lord. I kiss his hand. My letter will inform him of my mind. Farewell.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 1 — Salisbury. An open place
paragraphs: [Enter SHERIFF and halberdiers, with BUCKINGHAM, led to execution.]
BUCKINGHAM. Will King Richard not let me speak with him?
SHERIFF. No, my good lord. So be patient.

BUCKINGHAM. Hastings, and Edward's children, Grey, and Rivers, holy King Henry, and your fair son Edward, Vaughan, and all who have perished by underhanded, corrupted foul injustice — if your moody discontented souls through the clouds behold this present hour, even for revenge mock my destruction. This is All Souls' day, fellow, isn't it?
SHERIFF. It is.

BUCKINGHAM. Why, then All Souls' day is my body's doomsday. This is the day which, in King Edward's time, I wished might fall on me when I was found false to his children and his wife's allies. This is the day on which I wished to fall by the false faith of him whom I most trusted. This, this All Souls' day, to my fearful soul, is the determined deadline of my wrongs. That high All-Seer whom I dallied with has turned my feigned prayer on my head, and given in earnest what I begged in jest. Thus he forces the swords of wicked men to turn their own points into their masters' bosoms. Thus Margaret's curse falls heavy on my neck: "When he," she said, "shall split your heart with sorrow, remember Margaret was a prophetess." Come, lead me, officers, to the block of shame. Wrong has but wrong, and blame is the due of blame.
[Exit with officers.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 2 — Plain near Tamworth
paragraphs: [Enter RICHMOND, OXFORD, BLUNT, HERBERT, and others, with drum and colors.]

RICHMOND. Fellows in arms, and my most loving friends, bruised under the yoke of tyranny, thus far into the bowels of the land we have marched on without impediment. And here we receive from our father Stanley lines of fair comfort and encouragement. The wretched, bloody, and usurping boar, who spoiled your summer fields and fruitful vines, swills your warm blood like swill, and makes his trough in your gutted bosoms — this foul swine is now in the very center of this isle, near the town of Leicester, as we learn. From Tamworth to there is but one day's march. In God's name, cheerly on, courageous friends, to reap the harvest of perpetual peace by this one bloody trial of sharp war.
OXFORD. Every man's conscience is a thousand men, to fight against that guilty homicide.
HERBERT. I have no doubt his friends will turn to us.
BLUNT. He has no friends but those who are friends out of fear, who in his dearest need will fly from him.
RICHMOND. All for our advantage. Then in God's name, march. True hope is swift, and flies with swallow's wings. Kings it makes gods, and meaner creatures kings.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 3 — Bosworth Field
paragraphs: [Enter KING RICHARD in armor, with NORFOLK, RATCLIFFE and the Earl of SURREY, with others.]
KING RICHARD. Pitch our tent here, right here in Bosworth field. My Lord of Surrey, why do you look so sad?
SURREY. My heart is ten times lighter than my looks.
KING RICHARD. My lord of Norfolk.
NORFOLK. Here, most gracious sovereign.
KING RICHARD. Norfolk, we'll have to take some blows, won't we?
NORFOLK. We must both give and take, my loving lord.
KING RICHARD. Up with my tent! Here I'll lie tonight. But where tomorrow? Well, it's all the same. Who has counted the number of the traitors?
NORFOLK. Six or seven thousand is the most they have.

KING RICHARD. Why, our army triples that number. Besides, the King's name is a tower of strength, which their adverse faction lacks. Up with the tent! Come, noble gentlemen, let's survey the lay of the ground. Call for some men of sound judgment. Let's not lack discipline, make no delay, for, lords, tomorrow is a busy day.
[The tent is now ready. They exit.]
[Enter RICHMOND, Sir William Brandon, OXFORD, HERBERT, BLUNT, and others who pitch Richmond's tent.]

RICHMOND. The weary sun has made a golden setting, and by the bright track of his fiery chariot gives a sign of a fine day tomorrow. Sir William Brandon, you will bear my standard. Give me some ink and paper in my tent. I'll draw up the form and plan of our battle, assign each leader to his particular charge, and divide our small force in just proportion. My Lord of Oxford, you, Sir William Brandon, and you, Sir Walter Herbert, stay with me. The Earl of Pembroke keeps his regiment. Good Captain Blunt, take my good night to him, and by the second hour of the morning, ask the Earl to come see me in my tent. One more thing, good captain, do for me. Where is Lord Stanley quartered, do you know?
BLUNT. Unless I have mistaken his colors badly — which I'm sure I have not — his regiment lies at least half a mile south of the King's mighty force.
RICHMOND. If you can do it safely, sweet Blunt, find some good means to speak with him, and give him from me this very necessary note.
BLUNT. On my life, my lord, I'll undertake it. And so God give you quiet rest tonight.
RICHMOND. Good night, good Captain Blunt.
[Exit BLUNT.]
Come, gentlemen, let's confer about tomorrow's business. Into my tent. The dew is raw and cold.
[RICHMOND, BRANDON, HERBERT, and OXFORD withdraw into the tent. The others exit.]
[Enter to his tent KING RICHARD, RATCLIFFE, NORFOLK and CATESBY with Soldiers.]
KING RICHARD. What time is it?
CATESBY. It's supper time, my lord. It's nine o'clock.
KING RICHARD. I won't eat tonight. Give me some ink and paper. What, is my helmet visor easier than it was? And all my armor laid out in my tent?
CATESBY. It is, my liege, and all things are in readiness.
KING RICHARD. Good Norfolk, hurry to your post. Keep careful watch. Choose trusty sentinels.
NORFOLK. I go, my lord.
KING RICHARD. Be up with the lark tomorrow, gentle Norfolk.
NORFOLK. I promise you, my lord.
[Exit.]
KING RICHARD. Catesby!
CATESBY. My lord?
KING RICHARD. Send out a herald-at-arms to Stanley's regiment. Tell him to bring his force before sunrise, or else his son George will fall into the blind cave of eternal night.
[Exit CATESBY.]
Fill me a bowl of wine. Give me a watchman. Saddle white Surrey for the field tomorrow. See that my lances are sound, and not too heavy. Ratcliffe!
RATCLIFFE. My lord?
KING RICHARD. Did you see the melancholy Lord Northumberland?
RATCLIFFE. Thomas the Earl of Surrey and he, about twilight, went from troop to troop through the army, cheering up the soldiers.
KING RICHARD. So, I am satisfied. Give me a bowl of wine. I don't have the alertness of spirit nor the cheerfulness of mind I used to have. Set it down. Is ink and paper ready?
RATCLIFFE. It is, my lord.
KING RICHARD. Tell my guard to keep watch. Leave me. Ratcliffe, around midnight come to my tent and help me arm. Leave me, I say.
[Exit RATCLIFFE. RICHARD withdraws into his tent; attendant soldiers guard it.]
[Enter STANLEY Earl of Derby to RICHMOND in his tent.]
STANLEY. Fortune and victory sit upon your helmet!
RICHMOND. All comfort that the dark night can give be to you, noble father-in-law. Tell me, how is our loving mother?

STANLEY. I, by proxy, bless you from your mother, who prays continually for Richmond's good. So much for that. The silent hours are slipping by, and flaky darkness breaks in the east. In short, since the season demands it, prepare your battle early in the morning, and trust your fortune to the verdict of bloody strokes and deadly war. I, as I may — what I would do, I cannot — will, with the best advantage, deceive the time and aid you in this doubtful clash of arms. But I cannot be too openly on your side, lest, being seen, your brother, tender George, be executed in his father's sight. Farewell. The leisure and the fearful time cut short the ceremonious vows of love and the rich exchange of sweet conversation that such long-separated friends should dwell on. God give us leisure for these rites of love! Once more, goodbye. Be valiant, and may you succeed.

RICHMOND. Good lords, conduct him to his regiment. I'll try with troubled thoughts to take a nap, lest leaden sleep weigh me down tomorrow when I should mount with wings of victory. Once more, good night, kind lords and gentlemen.
[All but RICHMOND leave his tent.]
[Kneels.] O Thou, whose captain I count myself,
