look on my forces with a gracious eye. Put in their hands Thy bruising irons of wrath, that they may crush down with a heavy fall the usurping helmets of our adversaries. Make us Thy ministers of chastisement, that we may praise Thee in the victory. To Thee I commend my watchful soul before I let fall the windows of my eyes. Sleeping and waking, O, defend me still!
[Sleeps.]
[Enter the GHOST OF EDWARD, young Prince Edward, son to Henry the Sixth.]
GHOST OF EDWARD.
[To KING RICHARD.] Let me sit heavy on your soul tomorrow.
Think how you stabbed me in the prime of my youth at Tewkesbury. Therefore despair, and die!
[To RICHMOND.] Be cheerful, Richmond, for the wronged souls
of butchered princes fight on your behalf. King Henry's heir, Richmond, comforts you.
[Exit.]
[Enter the GHOST OF HENRY the Sixth.]
GHOST OF HENRY.
[To KING RICHARD.] When I was alive, my anointed body
was punched full of deadly holes by you. Think on the Tower and me. Despair, and die. Henry the Sixth bids you despair and die.
[To RICHMOND.] Virtuous and holy, may you be conqueror.
Henry, who prophesied that you would be king, comforts you in your sleep. Live, and flourish!
[Exit.]
[Enter the GHOST OF CLARENCE.]
GHOST OF CLARENCE.
[To KING RICHARD.] Let me sit heavy in your soul tomorrow,
I, who was washed to death with loathsome wine, poor Clarence, betrayed to death by your guile. Tomorrow in the battle think on me, and let your blunted sword fall. Despair, and die!
[To RICHMOND.] You offspring of the house of Lancaster,
the wronged heirs of York pray for you. Good angels guard your battle. Live, and flourish.
[Exit.]
[Enter the GHOSTS OF RIVERS, GREY and VAUGHAN.]
GHOST OF RIVERS.
[To KING RICHARD.] Let me sit heavy in your soul tomorrow,
Rivers, who died at Pomfret. Despair and die!
GHOST OF GREY.
[To KING RICHARD.] Think upon Grey, and let your soul despair!
GHOST OF VAUGHAN.
[To KING RICHARD.] Think upon Vaughan, and with guilty fear
let your lance fall. Despair and die!
ALL THREE.
[To RICHMOND.] Awake, and think our wrongs in Richard's heart
will conquer him. Awake, and win the day.
[They exit.]
[Enter the GHOST OF HASTINGS.]
GHOST OF HASTINGS.
[To KING RICHARD.] Bloody and guilty, awake in guilt,
and end your days in a bloody battle. Think on Lord Hastings. Despair and die!
[To RICHMOND.] Quiet untroubled soul, awake, awake.
Arm, fight, and conquer for fair England's sake.
[Exit.]
[Enter the GHOSTS of the two young Princes.]
GHOSTS OF PRINCES.
[To KING RICHARD.] Dream on your cousins smothered in the Tower.
Let us be lead within your heart, Richard, and weigh you down to ruin, shame, and death. Your nephews' souls bid you despair and die.
[To RICHMOND.] Sleep, Richmond, sleep in peace, and wake in joy.
Good angels guard you from the boar's harm. Live, and beget a happy race of kings. Edward's unhappy sons bid you flourish.
[They exit.]
[Enter the GHOST OF Lady ANNE, his wife.]
GHOST OF ANNE.
[To KING RICHARD.] Richard, your wife, the wretched Anne your wife,
who never slept a quiet hour with you, now fills your sleep with disturbance. Tomorrow in the battle think on me, and let your blunted sword fall. Despair and die!
[To RICHMOND.] You quiet soul, sleep a quiet sleep.
Dream of success and happy victory. Your enemy's wife prays for you.
[Exit.]
[Enter the GHOST OF BUCKINGHAM.]
GHOST OF BUCKINGHAM.
[To KING RICHARD.] I was the first to help you to the crown.

I was the last to feel your tyranny. O, in the battle think on Buckingham, and die in terror of your guilt. Dream on, dream on of bloody deeds and death. Fainting, despair. Despairing, yield your breath.
[To RICHMOND.] I died for hope before I could lend you aid,
but cheer your heart, and don't be dismayed. God and good angels fight on Richmond's side, and Richard falls at the height of all his pride.
[Exit.]
[KING RICHARD starts up out of his dream.]

KING RICHARD. Give me another horse! Bind up my wounds! Have mercy, Jesus! Wait! I was only dreaming. O coward conscience, how you afflict me! The lights burn blue. It's now dead midnight. Cold, fearful drops stand on my trembling flesh. What do I fear? Myself? There's no one else here. Richard loves Richard, that is, I am I. Is there a murderer here? No. Yes, I am. Then flee. What, from myself? Good reason why, in case I take revenge. What, myself upon myself? Alas, I love myself. Why? For any good that I have done to myself? O no, alas, I rather hate myself for the hateful deeds I have committed. I am a villain. Yet I lie, I am not. Fool, speak well of yourself. Fool, don't flatter. My conscience has a thousand separate tongues, and every tongue brings in a separate tale, and every tale condemns me as a villain. Perjury, perjury, in the highest degree. Murder, brutal murder, in the worst degree. All my sins, used in every degree, crowd to the bar, all crying "Guilty, guilty!" I shall despair. There is no one who loves me, and if I die no soul will pity me. And why should they, since I myself find in myself no pity for myself? I thought the souls of all whom I had murdered came to my tent, and each one threatened tomorrow's vengeance on the head of Richard.
[Enter RATCLIFFE.]
RATCLIFFE. My lord!
KING RICHARD. Damn! Who's there?
RATCLIFFE. Ratcliffe, my lord. It's I. The early village rooster has twice saluted the morning. Your friends are up and buckling on their armor.
KING RICHARD. O Ratcliffe, I have dreamed a fearful dream! What do you think, will our friends prove all true?
RATCLIFFE. No doubt, my lord.
KING RICHARD. O Ratcliffe, I fear, I fear!
RATCLIFFE. No, my good lord, don't be afraid of shadows.

KING RICHARD. By the apostle Paul, shadows tonight have struck more terror to the soul of Richard than the substance of ten thousand soldiers could, armored in proof and led by shallow Richmond. It is not yet near day. Come, go with me. Under our tents I'll play the eavesdropper, to see if any mean to shrink from me.
[Exit RICHARD and RATCLIFFE.]
[Enter the LORDS to RICHMOND in his tent.]
LORDS. Good morning, Richmond.
RICHMOND. Forgive me, lords and watchful gentlemen, that you have caught a tardy sluggard here.
LORDS. How have you slept, my lord?

RICHMOND. The sweetest sleep and fairest-omened dreams that ever entered a drowsy head have I had since your departure, my lords. I thought the souls of those whose bodies Richard had murdered came to my tent and cried for victory. I promise you, my heart is very joyful at the memory of so fair a dream. How far into the morning is it, lords?
LORDS. On the stroke of four.
RICHMOND. Why then, it is time to arm and give direction.
[His oration to his soldiers.]

More than I have said, loving countrymen, the leisure and pressure of the time forbid me to dwell on. Yet remember this: God, and our good cause, fight on our side. The prayers of holy saints and wronged souls, like high-built bulwarks, stand before our faces. Except for Richard, those whom we fight against would rather have us win than him whom they follow. For what is he they follow? Truly, gentlemen, a bloody tyrant and a murderer — one raised in blood, and one in blood established — one that made his way to come by what he has, and slaughtered those who were the means to help him — a base, foul stone, made precious by the foil of England's throne, where he is falsely placed — one who has ever been God's enemy. Then, if you fight against God's enemy, God will, in justice, protect you as his soldiers. If you sweat to put a tyrant down, you sleep in peace, the tyrant being slain. If you fight against your country's foes, your country's fat shall pay your pains as hire. If you fight to safeguard your wives, your wives shall welcome home the conquerors. If you free your children from the sword, your children's children shall repay it in your old age. Then, in the name of God and all these rights, advance your standards, draw your willing swords. For me, the ransom of my bold attempt shall be this cold corpse on the earth's cold face. But if I succeed, the gain of my attempt the least of you shall share his part of. Sound drums and trumpets boldly and cheerfully! God, and Saint George! Richmond and victory!
[They exit.]
[Enter KING RICHARD, RATCLIFFE and Soldiers.]
KING RICHARD. What did Northumberland say about Richmond?
RATCLIFFE. That he was never trained in arms.
KING RICHARD. He said the truth. And what said Surrey then?
RATCLIFFE. He smiled, and said, "The better for our purpose."
KING RICHARD. He was right, and so indeed it is.
[The clock strikes.]
Tell the clock there. Give me a calendar. Who saw the sun today?
RATCLIFFE. Not I, my lord.
KING RICHARD. Then it disdains to shine, for according to the book it should have braved the east an hour ago. A black day will it be to somebody. Ratcliffe!
RATCLIFFE. My lord?

KING RICHARD. The sun will not be seen today! The sky frowns and lowers upon our army. I wish these dewy tears were off the ground. Not shine today? Why, what's that to me more than to Richmond? For the very same heaven that frowns on me looks sadly upon him.
[Enter NORFOLK.]
NORFOLK. Arm, arm, my lord. The foe is advancing in the field.

KING RICHARD. Come, bustle, bustle! Trap up my horse. Call up Lord Stanley. Tell him to bring his force. I will lead forth my soldiers to the plain, and thus my battle shall be ordered: my vanguard shall be drawn out all in length, consisting equally of horse and foot. Our archers shall be placed in the middle. John, Duke of Norfolk, and Thomas, Earl of Surrey, shall have the leading of this foot and horse. With them directed, we will follow in the main battle, whose power on either side shall be well winged with our best horse. This, and Saint George to boot! What do you think, Norfolk?
NORFOLK. A good direction, warlike sovereign.
[He shows him a paper.]
I found this on my tent this morning.
KING RICHARD.
[Reads.] "Jockey of Norfolk, be not too bold.

For Dickon your master is bought and sold." A thing devised by the enemy. Go, gentlemen, every man to his post. Let not our babbling dreams frighten our souls. Conscience is just a word that cowards use, devised at first to keep the strong in awe. Our strong arms be our conscience, swords our law. March on. Join bravely. Let us at it pell-mell — if not to heaven, then hand in hand to hell.
[His oration to his army.]

What more shall I say than I have already declared? Remember whom you are to fight against — a pack of vagabonds, scoundrels, and runaways, a scum of Bretons and base lackey peasants, whom their over-stuffed country vomits forth to desperate adventures and certain destruction. While you sleep safe, they bring you unrest. While you have lands, and are blessed with beautiful wives, they would seize the one, defile the other. And who leads them but a paltry fellow, long kept in Brittany at our mother's expense? A milksop, one that never in his life felt as much cold as wet shoes in snow? Let's whip these stragglers over the seas again, lash away these overweening rags of France, these famished beggars, weary of their lives, who, but for dreaming on this foolish exploit, for want of means, poor rats, would have hanged themselves. If we are to be conquered, let men conquer us, and not these bastard Bretons, whom our fathers have beaten, bashed, and thumped in their own land, and left them on record as the heirs of shame. Shall these enjoy our lands? Lie with our wives, rape our daughters?
[Drum far off.]

Listen, I hear their drum. Fight, gentlemen of England! Fight, bold yeomen! Draw, archers, draw your arrows to the head! Spur your proud horses hard, and ride in blood! Astonish the sky with your broken lances!
[Enter a Messenger.]
What says Lord Stanley? Will he bring his force?
MESSENGER. My lord, he refuses to come.
KING RICHARD. Off with his son George's head!
NORFOLK. My lord, the enemy has passed the marsh. After the battle let George Stanley die.

KING RICHARD. A thousand hearts are great within my breast. Advance our standards! Set upon our foes! Our ancient war-cry of courage, fair Saint George, inspire us with the rage of fiery dragons! Upon them! Victory sits on our helmets.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 4 — Another part of the Field
paragraphs: [Alarum. Excursions. Enter NORFOLK and Soldiers; to him CATESBY.]

CATESBY. Rescue, my Lord of Norfolk, rescue, rescue! The King performs more wonders than a man, daring an opponent in every danger. His horse is killed, and he fights all on foot, seeking for Richmond in the throat of death. Rescue, fair lord, or else the day is lost!
[Exit NORFOLK and Soldiers.]
[Alarum. Enter KING RICHARD.]
KING RICHARD. A horse! A horse! My kingdom for a horse!
CATESBY. Withdraw, my lord. I'll help you to a horse.

KING RICHARD. Slave, I have set my life upon a cast, and I will stand the hazard of the die. I think there are six Richmonds in the field. Five have I killed today instead of him. A horse! A horse! My kingdom for a horse!
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 5 — Another part of the Field
paragraphs: [Alarum. Enter KING RICHARD and RICHMOND. They fight. RICHARD is killed. Then a retreat is sounded. RICHMOND exits, and RICHARD's body is carried off. Flourish. Enter RICHMOND, STANLEY Earl of Derby, bearing the crown, with other Lords and Soldiers.]
RICHMOND. God and your arms be praised, victorious friends! The day is ours. The bloody dog is dead.

STANLEY. Courageous Richmond, well have you acquitted yourself! Look, here, this long-usurped royalty I have plucked from the dead temples of this bloody wretch, to grace your brow with it. Wear it, enjoy it, and make much of it.
RICHMOND. Great God of heaven, say Amen to all! But tell me, is young George Stanley living?
STANLEY. He is, my lord, and safe in Leicester town, where, if it please you, we may now withdraw.
RICHMOND. What men of name are killed on either side?
STANLEY. John, Duke of Norfolk, Walter, Lord Ferrers, Sir Robert Brakenbury, and Sir William Brandon.

RICHMOND. Bury their bodies as befits their birth. Proclaim a pardon to the soldiers who fled, who in submission will return to us. And then, as we have taken the sacrament, we will unite the white rose and the red. Smile, heaven, upon this fair union, that has long frowned upon their enmity. What traitor hears me and does not say Amen? England has long been mad, and scarred herself. The brother blindly shed the brother's blood. The father rashly slaughtered his own son. The son, compelled, has been butcher to his sire. All this divided York and Lancaster, divided in their dire division. O, now let Richmond and Elizabeth, the true heirs of each royal house, by God's fair ordinance be joined together, and let their heirs, God, if it is Thy will, enrich the time to come with smooth-faced peace, with smiling plenty, and fair prosperous days. Blunt the edge of traitors, gracious Lord, who would bring back these bloody days again, and make poor England weep in streams of blood. Let them not live to taste this land's increase, that would with treason wound this fair land's peace. Now civil wounds are stopped, peace lives again. That she may long live here, God say Amen.
[They exit.]
